title: Kalkan: The State must take bold steps for a democratic solution
content:
Duran Kalkan, a member of the Abdullah Öcalan Academy of Social Sciences, gave a lengthy interview to Medya Haber TV.




Kalkan started by commemorating the martyrs of Rojhilat (Eastern Kurdistan), stressing that young people from Rojhilat had made significant contributions to the struggle for freedom in all four parts of Kurdistan. He emphasised the importance of upholding the legacy of those who had lost their lives in the struggle. 




Kalkan then talked about the current state of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




We publish excerpts from the interview.




The HPG has announced the names of the martyrs from Rojhilat, including those from Urmia. Perhaps we could begin from here.




For some time now, HPG-BIM has been announcing that young people from Rojhilat joined the freedom struggle being waged in Bakur (Northern Kurdistan) and Bashur (Southern Kurdistan), where they subsequently lost their lives. Announcements have been made group by group and city by city.




First and foremost, I commemorate these comrades, and through them all the martyrs of our freedom struggle, with respect, affection and gratitude. The youth of Rojhilatê Kurdistan resisted on their own soil while also making enormous contributions to the freedom struggle in the other parts of Kurdistan. They fought in Bakur, in Rojava and in Bashur. Wherever there was a struggle for freedom, they went there and took part. Moreover, they pursued this struggle in a manner characterised by the willingness to sacrifice their lives.




Our young people from Rojhilat are valuable, patriotic and conscious to this degree. Undoubtedly, this comes from the political consciousness of their society. They take a position according to the circumstances of the process. They never abandon their causes of freedom. Their Kurdish identity and their consciousness of Kurdistan are exceptionally strong. They are extremely courageous and self-sacrificing.




As someone who witnessed these events, I can say this very clearly: they truly made enormous contributions to both the struggle in Bakur and the struggle in Rojava. They were all exceptionally brave fighters, both women and men. They became commanders and fighters. They demonstrated every form of courage and sacrifice.




Our young people from Rojhilat must therefore understand these values and build their own consciousness upon them. They must know how to follow in the footsteps of these martyrs. We believe they will never stray from this path. They will struggle with great courage and sacrifice for the freedom of Rojhilat, for the freedom of all Kurdistan, and for the democratisation of Iran and the Middle East. Our people in Rojhilat should be proud of their martyrs. Every one of them is a monument to honour. These young women and men remained truly devoted and loyal to their homeland and their people. These heroes must always be a source of pride. We must draw strength from them.




On this basis, I once again commemorate our martyrs from Rojhilat with respect and gratitude. I salute their families and wish success to the freedom and democracy struggle being waged by our people in Rojhilat.




Let’s talk about the Peace and Democratic Society Process. There are assessments suggesting that new developments have taken place or are about to take place. Is this the case? To what extent do you agree? In the previous programme, the assessments focused more on the existence of a deadlock.




Once again, I would like to respectfully salute the historic resistance of Imralı and Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan]. The Imralı resistance continues to produce solutions and bring about developments.




The Peace and Democratic Society Process, which began with the call of 27 February 2025, has clearly reached a very important point. However, the situation is fluctuating. There are positive statements, but there are also pessimistic ones.




Recently, positive statements have come from various circles. Hopefully, things will turn out as they have said. What else can we say? Our leadership has also made clear the position of our movement. It assessed all these developments and took the statements seriously. It issued its own statement to ensure that the situation was properly understood and, furthermore, to open the way for new developments and steps to be taken.




The statement was very clear and understandable. It set out our movement's and leadership's position regarding the process, as well as what we have done and the steps we have taken. In doing so, it demonstrated that those who cheaply accuse our leadership and portray it as an obstacle are wrong. This is truly a great insult and an injustice.




We have not asked for anything for ourselves. Leader Apo is continuing the process as its chief negotiator. Everyone is making assessments, saying, "This must begin from the top, starting with the leadership." We have never said anything of the sort. We have said just one thing: only Leader Apo can bring this process to a successful conclusion. Therefore, if Leader Apo is able to work, live and lead freely, this process will succeed.




Those participating in this process presumably want it to succeed. If that is genuinely the case, and if they want success, we have already shown them the way to achieve it. This was the most correct and natural course of action. Legally, it was also the easiest thing to implement.




Some people say, "That is very difficult, it is the most difficult option, society would react negatively.” There is no truth to this. All of it is fabricated. They say they are conducting surveys and public opinion polls. They claim that there are negative reactions towards Leader Apo from this or that section of society. Of course, you say all sorts of things about him every single day. You do not even allow him to say a single word or express his thoughts to Turkish society. A campaign of vilification has been going on for 28 years, even 40 years. And then they claim that this or that section of Turkish society would react negatively. These reactions have been manufactured. They are not the genuine reactions of society.




Let him be given the opportunity to speak. Let Leader Apo also put forward his own position and views. Then we will see what happens. If they genuinely believe what they are saying, they should not be afraid. Why are they afraid, then? Why do they continue to prevent him from speaking freely? For this reason, none of these arguments are realistic.




There is no such social pressure. The situation is entirely connected to the mentality and policies of the leadership, the state and the government. They have still not changed their policies or their mentality. They say, "Yes, we are committed to the process, and democratisation is necessary." But they are making no effort and taking no action in accordance with what this actually requires. They have not explained this to Turkish society. They have not created the conditions for Leader Apo to work in response to what he and our movement have done. They are not creating those conditions.




What they provide is extremely limited and insufficient. Leader Apo criticised the situation by saying, "I am being asked to swim in a pool without water.” In this respect, we have asked for what is reasonable. He has been held in Imralı for 28 years. Legally, he should already have been released. He should have been able to benefit from the right to hope (

umut hakkı

). Devlet Bahçeli also said this. He issued a call, saying, "Come and speak in Parliament.” We are not asking for anything else. The statements and calls made by MHP Chairman Devlet Bahçeli should simply be implemented. But they have not been implemented.




Our people and friends must not be misled




In this regard, surely there can be no fault in our stating that something which has not happened has not happened. Let us make this absolutely clear. This is what we asked for. It is Leader Apo's right. It is the most legally appropriate and straightforward measure that could be taken. Politically, it is also the reality that would enable this process to be conducted most successfully and brought to a successful conclusion. Nobody else can do it. We explained all this, and the situation was perfectly understandable. We continue to maintain that this remains valid.




So, what might the current situation mean? It was announced that Leader Apo had been saying for some time, "Let my status first be clarified, and then I will move to a new location.” Now his location has been changed, and this has been announced. It has been stated that he has moved to a new place. Apparently, he had already been meeting the visiting delegation in that area for some time. But this is not some major development or anything particularly significant. It is the place where Leader Apo was initially taken when he first arrived, and where he remained until other comrades were brought there. The place was demolished and rebuilt. Let us say that it is a somewhat larger facility within the prison, with improved physical facilities. There has been no change in his status. Nor has there been any substantial change in his working conditions as a result. It has been stated that such changes will take place. Some people have made statements to this effect. As we said, hopefully that will happen. We are waiting to see whether it genuinely happens or not.




Everything is achieved through struggle. Our people and our friends must not be misled. Nothing of this kind has actually happened or been realised yet. These changes will take place only to the extent that we continue our struggle for freedom and democracy; to the extent that we spread an understanding of democracy, its requirements and its importance throughout Turkish society; and to the extent that we develop closer alliances and relations with the peoples of the world and advance our struggle.




Let us make one thing clear: our leadership has already issued its statement. Indeed, through the steps we have taken as a movement, we have brought matters to this point. As things stand, the factors that could lead to armed conflict with Turkey have been eliminated, provided that no deliberate and planned military attack is launched. We have removed these factors. In this sense, disarmament has taken place to this extent and at this level. There is nothing further that we can do in a similar way beyond this point.




From here onwards, the responsibility genuinely lies with Turkey. For this to happen, the necessary political and legal requirements must be fulfilled. The government and the state must take steps. If they are going to implement the framework law they have established, Leader Apo must be the one to lead this process. They must clarify Leader Apo's status. Discussions are currently taking place about the establishment of a council. They said, "We are establishing the higher council and subordinate committees envisaged by the law.” In that case, this council must be officially announced.




The next step is the enactment of freedom laws




Leader Apo must genuinely be enabled to work freely and effectively. On the other hand, as a necessary part of this process, steps must be taken to democratise the Republic. The conditions necessary for democratic politics must be established. Turkey's political and legal environment must be democratised through concrete legal and political measures. Everything is being made dependent on our leadership. People claim that our leadership has not included certain groups and is obstructing the process. 




There is no truth to this.




There are comrades who have burned their weapons and are waiting. Their names have been announced repeatedly, day after day. Suppose even one person were to return under the current circumstances. Yes, perhaps the authorities say, "We have postponed the implementation of that law," but they also say, "You cannot come alone; you must bring everyone with you.” 




How could that person possibly bring everyone? Where would they get the power to do so? Furthermore, even if someone returned, would they genuinely be able to participate in democratic politics as a Kurd, with their own identity? Would they be able to engage in political activity? They would immediately be arrested and imprisoned. Under the existing laws and conditions, they would face the most severe forms of repression. This is perfectly clear because nothing has changed.




Therefore, the next step is now the enactment of freedom laws and the implementation of measures to democratise Turkey. We are not saying that these measures should be implemented simply so that we can benefit from them. It will not be only the Kurds who benefit from this. In fact, the Turkish people will benefit the most from a democratic Turkey. All of Turkish society will benefit. We are not asking for anything exclusively for the benefit of the Kurds or PKK members. We are asking for something that will benefit everyone.




Nothing could be clearer than this.




Consequently, the process has genuinely reached this stage. The path must now be opened for democratic politics. Steps towards democratisation must be taken. Looking at the current circumstances, the dangers still remain. What will protect Turkey from these dangers is the implementation of these measures, and they must be implemented quickly. This is what needs to happen.




Will these steps be taken? Will they be implemented? We will see.




They say they are "determined". They speak of democratisation. We hope that these commitments will become reality. As a movement, on the basis of Leader Apo's calls, we have taken the decisions that we believe are necessary. We remain determined to implement them at all times. There has been no retreat on our part.

title: Michel Kokoreff: We are witnessing the political awakening of a generation in France
content:
The protests initiated by high school and university students in France have gone beyond problems within the education system, evolving into a broader social movement against social inequalities, neoliberal policies and the State's increasingly repressive measures.




Police interventions against student demonstrations have intensified debates in the country concerning democratic rights and freedoms. Meanwhile, the rise of the far right across Europe and the crisis facing capitalism have also become major issues on the political agenda.




French sociologist Professor Michel Kokoreff, who teaches at Paris 8 University, spoke to ANF about the student protests in France, police violence, the social consequences of neoliberal policies and the rise of the far right in Europe.




For several weeks, high school and university students have been mobilising in France. Beyond demands related to education, what do these mobilisations reveal about the social and political tensions currently affecting French society?




It's always difficult to answer because the movement is still ongoing, so inevitably, this is a somewhat immediate analysis. However, it is nevertheless informed by, as you rightly mentioned, around ten different studies, since France has been shaken for roughly ten years by a number of social movements that have been somewhat unprecedented in their format, composition and political consequences.




What this reveals, in my view, above all, is the political awakening of a generation. The generational awakening of high school students from working-class backgrounds, who attend schools in peripheral areas. For example, in the Paris region, in the department of Seine-Saint-Denis, what is sometimes called the 

peripheral school system

: that is, a school system that is much less well-funded than schools located within the city limits of Paris. And this awakening has manifested itself through a rather explosive mixture of joy and anger.




Joy has been expressed, in particular, through the many banners and placards that appeared during demonstrations. They were often very inventive, often remarkably perceptive, full of irony.  At the same time, there has been anger regarding teaching conditions, their deterioration, the shortage of teachers, the extremely high temperatures in summer and the freezing conditions in winter due to a lack of proper equipment. In doing so, these young people have taken up a number of demands that trade unions have been putting forward for around ten years, particularly following the reform of the so-called Blanquer baccalaureate in 2018. These demands had not been heard, but this time they have benefited from considerably greater visibility. And this combination of joy, this cocktail of joy, anger and determination, expressed through blockades, particularly of a number of high schools, and these confrontational actions, has gone viral on social media.




We therefore saw university students initially joining the movement, so to speak, with their own demands, but also out of solidarity. Other sectors of French society and the world of work followed, particularly in the public sector, but not exclusively. Gradually, and we will undoubtedly come back to this, this high school and university student movement became a societal movement, perhaps more than a social movement in the traditional sense of one organised by trade unions. It triggered a political crisis at the highest level of the State. This was due, firstly, to the absence of any response for 15 days, the silence of the ministers responsible, namely the Minister of National Education and the Minister of Higher Education. There was no response; there was silence for 15 days. Fifteen days is a long time. And above all, there was what the Minister of the Interior described as repression carried out "without restraint" by law enforcement agencies and the police. There were no instructions to show restraint towards these young minors, many of whom were just 14 or 15 years old.




This resulted in brutal interventions, mutilations, hands being torn off, people losing an eye, and, more generally, people being traumatised. Obviously, a number of images also went viral on social media. These images provided an indication of the movement itself, but also exposed the brutality of police interventions. In a way, we could also speak of the cynicism of politicians, both men and women, who justified this police violence in the name of fighting urban violence. So perhaps this is also what deeply shocked part of French society: a kind of inhumanity, or dehumanisation, on the part of those in power, who, unable to find an answer to the anger of high school students, could offer nothing other than a policy of police batons.




In your book 

La Diagonale de la rage

 (

The Diagonal of Rage

), you analyse social movements in France since May 1968. How would you place the current mobilisations within this history? Are we witnessing the emergence of a new generation of protesters?




Undoubtedly. This is what we call Generation Z: essentially young minors, between the ages of 14 and 19, attending high school. We thought this generation had been completely lobotomised, alienated by smartphones, social media and digital platforms, concerned only with their image, their appearance and brands. Yet we are discovering that they are politically aware, as I mentioned earlier, clear-sighted about their teaching conditions, and also driven by a strong sense of injustice.




A sense of injustice regarding their own situation, a sense of injustice regarding inequalities, and also a sense of injustice in relation to the police violence I mentioned. There is also a sense of injustice regarding the different treatment they receive as a population of immigrant descent, whether first or second generation. In France, they are commonly referred to as Black people and Arabs. This is a colloquial expression, but not necessarily a derogatory one. So, indeed, nobody expected this movement, including the most observant and perceptive experts of the social landscape, among whom I count myself. I would never have bet on this movement at the beginning of September.




We could certainly sense that anger was growing in France, particularly regarding the rising cost of living and fuel prices, as well as what we call the energy crisis, which has affected many countries in the geopolitical context you are familiar with. But we did not expect this anger to erupt here and crystallise in this particular place, in these working-class high schools, among these young people.




Because of this unexpected nature, we can also emphasise how unprecedented the movement is. In other words, it is not simply that nobody expected it to emerge here. We could have imagined that it would follow a fairly traditional repertoire of action, what we might call a fairly traditional grammar of protest, at least in France. But this movement is unprecedented, and we must continue to speak about it in the present tense.




If we look back around twenty years, it was primarily young people from the middle and upper classes, the lower middle class, and sometimes those experiencing social downgrading, who were at the forefront of protests. Working-class urban young people, on the other hand, are more commonly associated with riots following the deaths of young people as a result of police intervention, as was the case with the most recent riots in 2023.




So, indeed, we are seeing blockades, relatively joyful demonstrations, young people who are not politically affiliated, who do not belong to political parties and who maintain a certain distance from traditional organisations and trade unions. Somewhat like the Yellow Vests, this movement has developed its own particular repertoire of action. But this movement has also been unprecedented because of the repression it has faced. For example, there were 8,000 arrests in just three weeks, an entirely unprecedented figure.




You have also devoted several studies to police violence. From the Yellow Vests to student mobilisations, the issue of repression keeps coming up. How do you analyse this evolution in security policies? Can it be seen as a sign of an increasingly authoritarian hardening of the French State?




Many people have observed this. Many commentators and researchers have indeed pointed to what they describe as a drift, particularly through the use of exceptional measures that are gradually becoming normalised, and not simply through repression itself.




The so-called "rioters pay" law (

loi casseurs-payeurs

) is, in many respects, a law that restricts civil liberties. In other words, it calls fundamental constitutional freedoms into question, including the freedom to demonstrate and the freedoms of expression and opinion. Perhaps we should recall that police violence, understood as State violence, has a long history in France, one of which we cannot necessarily be very proud.




Without going as far back as the nineteenth century, this is what I attempted to do in another book you mentioned, entitled 

Police Violence: Genealogy of State Violence

, published in 2021. In that book, I traced this cycle of State violence back to 1945, during the first demonstrations demanding Algeria's independence, which ended in a massacre. This was followed by other massacres during the Algerian War, on 17 October 1961, on 8 February 1962 in Charonne, and in March and May 1967 in Guadeloupe.




There is a long history here, characterised by several elements: first, extraordinary levels of violence; second, protection and cover-ups by the hierarchy and the ministers responsible for overseeing the police; and third, impunity. We could even identify a fourth characteristic: forgetting, amnesia, as history repeats itself. One could quite easily argue that the roadmap of Macron-style neoliberalism consists, on the one hand, of implementing counter-reforms that, for example, dismantle labour rights, increase precariousness and institutionalise it, while also dismantling and stripping public services of their resources.




At the same time, the only thing expected of the population is obedience. And if people have the audacity to take to the streets and challenge these neoliberal policies, they are met with repression. This is precisely what we have witnessed over the past ten years.




One particularly clear example is the movement against pension reform in 2023, which was ultimately passed by the National Assembly through the use of Article 49.3 of the French Constitution. So what does this tell us? It tells us something about a weak government, a fragile government. It is not only a government that wants to bring young people and all forms of protest into line, rather than prioritising dialogue; it also reveals the fragility of those in power. And this creates the impression that we are no longer entirely living in democratic societies based on the Fordist compromise, dialogue with trade unions and negotiations with civil society.




Some people go as far as speaking of fascist moments, and we are moving towards authoritarian regimes. Of course, France is not China. I will not comment on Turkey, so as not to say something inaccurate, but we still have the possibility of demonstrating, even if doing so is becoming increasingly difficult. We find ourselves at a kind of crossroads, and the people involved are quite conscious of this. They have the feeling that they are writing a page of history. 




There was a placard that expressed this ironically. Obviously, it should be understood in a tongue-in-cheek sense, but nevertheless: Fourth Reich or Sixth Republic?




I would like to ask you some questions about the rise of the far right in Europe. In France, Germany, Italy and several other European countries, the far right is gaining ground. This progress is taking place against a backdrop of economic, social and political crises. In your opinion, is it a symptom of a deeper crisis in the European political and social model?




Not necessarily of the European social and political model, but rather of a kind of crisis of globalisation, a crisis of neoliberal capitalism, which produces the same effects wherever it takes hold. The same causes produce the same effects. Young people in Greece, for example, are subjected to the same policies, the same precariousness, potentially the same contempt and the same repression as young people in France and Italy.




What is at stake, without pretending to be Lenin or Trotsky, is, in my view, a crisis of an economic model that fails to produce the expected results for the population, according to the famous trickle-down theory, whereby everyone is ultimately supposed to benefit from profits. On the contrary, the figures clearly show an almost obscene maximisation of multinational corporations' profits and the distribution of these profits among shareholders. These figures are quite damning when it comes to demonstrating how a minority is able to benefit from the supposed trickle-down effect or from economic activity, whereas the overwhelming majority does not benefit from it at all.




In France, for example, we have observed a 0.1% decline in gross domestic product over the past three months, whereas GDP increased by 0.4% in the United Kingdom and 0.6% in Spain. Normally, France tends to be around the European average. This shows that capital is lazy. Capital is not investing, despite the profits that are being redistributed, but not reinvested, and despite the €166 billion that the State has transferred to the private sector. This is an indication, alongside other short-term economic indicators such as inflation, that the proposed economic model is not working. It is not generating the expected level of economic activity and, naturally, it is fuelling anger, frustration and the impoverishment of the population.




In a way, the other major component of authoritarian capitalism is repression. However, there is no guarantee that repression will actually neutralise protest movements. Furthermore, it is facing considerable criticism, not only in France and not only from the parliamentary opposition. Somehow, both pillars of authoritarian capitalism, or of the security-oriented liberal society, are limping.




We are talking about a crisis of globalisation and a crisis of capitalism, alongside the rise of the far right. But what is the role of the left? Left-wing parties in France and Germany are often criticised. It has been said that they do not really have their own policies to counter this phenomenon. Do you agree with that?




It is certainly true that the crisis of globalisation, to call it that, encourages a tendency towards identity-based withdrawal. It encourages patriotism, so to speak. And, obviously, this is precisely the political territory occupied by the far right, which we are familiar with. Of course, it is not entirely identical in Germany, France, India or even the United States. But it is clear that the far right is thriving on the basis of a crisis of globalisation and using it to promote national preference, to borrow Marine Le Pen's expression. This is something that high school students understand perfectly well when they say, "Young people show the finger to the National Front" (

La jeunesse emmerde le Front National

). They are deliberately using the former name of the far-right party so as not to fall into the trap of the superficial normalisation of  the new name, National Rally.




Obviously, there is an extremely powerful media propaganda operation at work, due to a kind of monopolistic tendency within the media landscape, personified by Mr Bolloré. This monopolistic tendency and this media propaganda mean that, throughout the day and across news programmes and newspapers, we hear primarily the voice of the National Rally or, occasionally, that of the police union Alliance.




So, in this context, what does the left do? In a way, the left is doing what it can, since it is nevertheless subject to considerable criticism and discrediting. Even the second-highest-ranking figure in the State, the President of the Senate, has raised the possibility of dissolving La France Insoumise, on the grounds that this organisation, which is not a political party, allegedly encouraged looting and acts of vandalism, particularly on 17 October. This is part of the government's vocabulary surrounding urban violence, through which it conflates the parliamentary left, described as radical, with the ultra-left, whose actual identity is not particularly clear. So, in this context, it is clear that two political forces are benefiting from this situation of political crisis.




On the one hand, there is the National Rally, which can point to its lack of responsibility for governing and therefore criticise the government currently in power, while advocating racist, xenophobic and Islamophobic national preference policies. At the same time, essentially, it offers nothing different from the traditional right when it comes to economic policy. And then, on the other hand, we have La France Insoumise, which is calling for a Sixth Republic and advocating a very ambitious programme of reforms.




We have a kind of polarisation of the political landscape. This is not a polarisation between two extremes that would somehow converge, because we cannot equate the National Rally and La France Insoumise, for a whole range of reasons, but primarily for reasons of common sense.




Meanwhile, Emmanuel Macron's strategy has been to break this bipolarisation and establish a kind of three-party or three-pole system, comprising the right-wing central bloc, the far right and the radical left. That strategy has not worked, and today the right, the so-called central bloc, is in a very difficult position. We can see one indication of this in opinion polls and voting intentions, which are very low. But we can also clearly see that the traditional right, which is nevertheless becoming increasingly close to the far right, is struggling to make its voice heard.




So, broadly speaking, the situation is full of uncertainties. This is what we hear and what we see. There have been elections in 1998 and 1997, but ultimately, nothing is certain.

title: Social siege in Yüksekova: Children, women and youth targeted - Part Two
content:
Allegations of child sexual abuse, harassment and sexual assault against women in Hakkari (Colemêrg), particularly in Yüksekova (Gever), have brought long-standing social problems in the district back into focus. 




The first part of this feature can be read 

here

.  




The sexual assault cases involving the names of Necat Koparan, Eren Oğuz and Nevzat Çiftçi reveal a situation that society in Yüksekova (Gever) can no longer ignore. Necat Koparan and Eren Oğuz are named in the case involving the alleged sexual assault of a 13-year-old child, based on the child's testimony. Koparan is a wedding musician and also a security guard. Oğuz is a school bus driver. Several women have also made allegations of sexual assault, harassment, threats and blackmail against wedding musician Nevzat Çiftçi.




The fact that these individuals continue to perform at weddings raises serious questions for society. If reports that Eren Oğuz is still transporting students are accurate, how should families who entrust their children to school buses respond to this situation?




Why, then, are these two wedding musicians still invited to perform at weddings despite the allegations of sexual assault, harassment and other incidents surrounding them and the network of troubling relationships in which their names appear? Do wedding hosts, families and organizers never ask themselves: "Have you no shame? On what grounds are you inviting these individuals to your weddings?" How can it be considered normal for them to continue performing as though nothing has happened when such serious allegations have been made?




Kurdish weddings are gatherings that bring together families, relatives, neighbors and local communities, with their own distinctive social bonds. Families organize the weddings, and people from villages and neighborhoods attend. Why, then, is there not greater scrutiny when these individuals are invited to perform? Why do families, relatives, shopkeepers, local politicians and respected community figures not respond more strongly? Are a few press statements and messages of condemnation enough?




Another issue raised in videos and during our interviews concerns the presence of soldiers and police officers at neighborhood weddings, particularly around these two wedding musicians. What are specialist sergeants and police officers doing at Kurdish weddings where families, relatives and neighbors gather? How do they attend these events? Through whom do they establish connections with these circles? What is the nature of their relationships? Why are these environments, where women and children have reported harassment and sexual assault, not being questioned?




Another important question is why society's own mechanisms of accountability are not being activated. What position are families, villages, neighborhoods, shopkeepers, local politicians and respected community figures taking in response to these incidents? Why are individuals facing such serious allegations still invited to weddings? Is no one willing to question their continued performances?




Destroyed neighborhoods and a new social siege




The collapse of the resolution process and the intensification of clashes after 2015 brought many cities across Kurdistan under siege in every aspect of life. Treating developments in Hakkari (Colemêrg) and its districts, particularly Yüksekova, as isolated incidents prevents us from understanding the broader picture. The destruction of neighborhoods during urban clashes cannot be viewed merely as a consequence of armed conflict. We must also recognize that neighborhood culture and collective memory were targeted through this destruction.




The new buildings constructed in place of demolished neighborhoods, together with the unfamiliar way of life introduced into the town, were intended to sever people's connections with their culture and roots. This was not simply a matter of constructing new buildings. It was an intervention in the shared culture of a town, relations between neighbors, neighborhood solidarity and society's collective capacity to respond. Displacing people from their living spaces and forcing them into a different way of life was also part of this policy.




How, then, was this siege carried out? As clashes intensified during the period of self-rule, local political representation, broader political structures, the press, local cultural solidarity networks and all organized structures within society were targeted. These structures were first weakened and placed under siege. The social fabric of the town was then targeted. Yüksekova is one of the clearest examples of this process. Attacks on local political structures and social solidarity networks took place alongside the destruction of neighborhoods. Women's organizations and local solidarity networks were also subjected to this siege. The aim was to deprive people of their own means of solidarity and force them to accept an imposed way of life. This was how special warfare manifested itself in urban areas.




As neighborhoods were demolished, those that remained were surrounded by fear. But what would replace the dismantled social networks and structures of solidarity? This is where another dimension of special warfare policies came into play. The resulting vacuum was not filled spontaneously. A new mentality based on ostentation and consumption, alien to the town's culture and people's way of life, was introduced. Luxury cafés, restaurants and similar establishments became the visible face of this transformation. The aim was to encourage people to aspire to an artificial, extravagant world to which they did not belong and which they could not economically afford. Driving people into financial hardship through consumption, gradually distancing them from their culture and roots, became an important part of this policy.




Young people, who represent the future of society, are particularly targeted at this point. One of the most troubling examples is the practice of renting out bank accounts and International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), an issue widely discussed today in Hakkari, particularly Yüksekova. Young people encouraged to aspire to extravagant lifestyles, while facing unemployment and economic hardship, are drawn into illicit financial networks in an effort to survive or maintain their place in this consumer culture. Many of them are children of families who migrated from rural areas. Individuals involved in money laundering, drug trafficking and illegal financial transactions establish relationships with young people in these establishments and persuade them to allow their bank accounts to be used in exchange for various promises.




How does this system operate? Illicit funds are introduced into the financial system through the bank accounts of hundreds of young people in exchange for small payments and various promises. The most striking aspect is that while those who embezzle funds, plunder state resources and launder billions of lira move about freely, unemployed and desperate young people, the weakest links in this chain, are made scapegoats. Young people who allow their accounts to be used for small sums are prosecuted, arrested and deprived of their futures. Today, hundreds of young people are dealing with these investigations and court cases. Reducing the issue of IBAN renting to a few young people's desire to make easy money means ignoring the relationships behind this illicit network.




The fact that young people are being drawn into drug addiction and criminalized through such networks is no coincidence. The social solidarity built through tribal and kinship relations in Yüksekova, along with the collective accountability and shared conscience that this solidarity once fostered, is now being eroded. Yüksekova has not only been subjected to the security policies of a war that has continued for many years. Today, it is also experiencing another form of siege through special warfare practices. The district is being pushed away from political participation and social she aim of forcing people into silence and making them accustomed to what is happening around them.




Our interviews with shopkeepers, politicians and human rights defenders also reveal this picture. The developments in the district cannot be regarded as unrelated, isolated crimes or judicial cases. The town's culture, economy and young people are under systematic siege. The aim is to render society incapable of protecting its own children and young people against these destructive special warfare policies.




The sexual assault, threats and blackmail cases involving the two wedding musicians mentioned earlier, as well as security guards and law enforcement personnel, must also be examined within this framework. Treating these increasingly widespread incidents, particularly those concentrated around the two local musicians, merely as individual crimes would mean ignoring the social relationships connecting those involved and the space they are allowed to occupy within society. Protecting young people, women and children requires questioning these relationships and recognizing the impact of special warfare policies in this sphere.




It is also noticeable that songs passed down through thousands of years of Kurdish collective memory are performed differently at weddings attended by these two local musicians. Does the style represented particularly by security guard and musician Necat Koparan, through examples such as "Keçika Instagramê," which lack cultural value and promote an aspirational lifestyle, truly belong at our weddings and celebrations? This is something we must question. We need to develop a collective social response to protect our culture, songs and weddings against this kind of cultural degradation. The criminal incidents surrounding these musicians cannot be considered separately from the changes taking place in the cultural sphere. Warning young people against the figures promoting this culture of imitation and the relationships they establish is an important part of the broader social struggle.




Another significant issue in Yüksekova concerns the traps set through longstanding tribal traditions and attempts to manipulate tribal structures. Loan sharking targeting shopkeepers experiencing financial difficulties has become particularly widespread in recent years. Shopkeepers we interviewed said that loan sharking had never been as widespread, or as openly presented as legitimate, as it is today.




How, then, can individuals involved in loan sharking and criminal networks be presented to society as tribal elders? The central issue here is the exploitation of longstanding tribal culture, traditions of solidarity and the principle of protecting members of the community. Using the name of a tribe to shield someone who has committed a crime contradicts the very essence of this tradition. A closer examination of these incidents reveals that we are not talking about people who preserve tribal culture and Kurdish customs, but individuals who exploit tribal names for personal gain while engaging in loan sharking and other criminal activities. These individuals use their access to readily available cash and the relationships they have established to secure social standing. Their appearances alongside law enforcement officers at official events and their willingness to pose for photographs are also part of this attempt to gain legitimacy. The issue is not tribal tradition itself, but the exploitation of that tradition to conceal criminal relationships and accumulate power. This is another dimension of special warfare policies that undermine the social fabric.




One example can be found in the complaints filed by women against wedding musician Nevzat Çiftçi. Statements by women reported in the press describe how they were allegedly threatened through relatives and subjected to blackmail in an attempt to force them to withdraw their complaints. What is particularly striking is how kinship relations are transformed into instruments of pressure to silence women and cover up crimes. We must also question what happens when social solidarity and family ties are used to silence women rather than protect them.




Our interviews with shopkeepers, local politicians and community leaders have also shown how special warfare policies, experienced in many cities across Kurdistan, have manifested themselves particularly in Yüksekova. The picture that emerges goes far beyond a handful of criminal incidents. It reveals a siege extending from the destruction of neighborhoods to the recruitment of young people into IBAN networks, from loan sharking and the exploitation of tribal relationships to threats against women and cultural erosion. Faced with these developments, society must rebuild its own mechanisms of solidarity and develop a collective response capable of protecting young people, women and children. Without a social struggle against this siege, it will not be possible to prevent these developments.




Society must now ask itself some difficult questions. Whom are we protecting, and for what reasons? What relationships are we remaining silent to preserve? Can we ignore someone's actions because of their tribe, wealth, connections or influence? If we genuinely defend our social values, we must also take a stand against those who exploit them. We must not hesitate to confront these individuals with the truth, expose their actions and oppose them within social life.




The time for silence, turning a blind eye and accommodating these practices is over. Yüksekova must take responsibility for its own future and develop a united social struggle against this siege.

title: Government invokes ‘bullet costs’ but ignores workers in peace process
content:
The Ministry of Health's proposed budget for 2027 will be discussed by the Parliamentary Planning and Budget Committee today, Monday. Ahead of the discussions, Diren Can Kaya, a member of the Istanbul-Aksaray Branch Executive Board of the Health and Social Services Workers' Union (SES), spoke about the unequal distribution of budget allocations, the resources transferred to private capital through city hospitals and the problems facing healthcare workers.




Kaya highlighted inequalities in budget allocations, saying that a total of 3.3 trillion Turkish lira had been allocated to security and defence spending, while only 1 trillion 196.6 billion lira had been earmarked for healthcare. Kaya said that the budget deficit had reached 4.1 trillion lira and that a large proportion of the budget was being directed towards interest payments and security policies.







 







Even during the peace process, workers have not benefited from the budget




Kaya recalled that the government's response to their demand for “A budget for health and education, not war” in previous years had been to ask, “Do you know how much a bullet costs?” Referring to figures released by the Ministry of Treasury and Finance, Kaya emphasised the importance of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Kaya said that the 40-year war had cost workers in Turkey 2.3 trillion dollars: “Figures released by the Ministry of Finance show that 2.3 trillion dollars came out of the pockets of workers in Turkey during the 40-year war. Despite nearly two years of discussions about democratic society and peace, we see that the current budget has brought no benefits to workers. Yet these resources could have been used to establish healthcare and community centres in cities, providing services in people's mother tongues, rather than being spent on security policies. Domestic peace can only be established through policies that benefit the people.”




Kaya also highlighted shortcomings in primary healthcare, saying that deficiencies in services designed to prevent illness and provide care for conditions that do not require hospitalisation must be addressed. Kaya also pointed to the barriers preventing sick prisoners from accessing healthcare and said that the budget should be structured to guarantee their right to treatment.




‘The current system creates artificially stimulated demand for healthcare’




Kaya said that while 1.5 trillion liras had been allocated to curative healthcare services, preventive healthcare had not received an adequate share of the budget. Criticising a budget policy focused on treating illnesses rather than preventing them, Kaya said: “What we have is not really a Ministry of Health budget, but rather a ‘Ministry of Illness’ budget. Looking at the budgets over the past three years, we see only minimal increases, with figures of 6.2, 6.9 and 7.2. However, as the Health and Social Services Workers' Union, we emphasise that the existing problems in healthcare cannot be resolved unless its share of the budget rises above 10 percent.”




Kaya also criticised the city hospital model, saying that resources allocated from the healthcare budget through the Build-Operate-Transfer model were being channelled to private capital and what Kaya described as “illness lobbies”.




Kaya said: “With the resources transferred to city hospitals, 300 new healthcare facilities with 600 beds each could have been established. Similarly, the budget allocated to city hospitals over 25 years could have been used to rebuild approximately 900 hospitals. The current system constantly directs people towards emergency departments and hospitals, creating ‘artificially stimulated demand for healthcare’. Patients are being deprived of their right to healthcare.”




‘There is a huge workforce waiting for healthcare appointments’




Kaya emphasised that doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers were not responsible for the failures of a healthcare system that produces illness rather than health. Kaya also acknowledged that the union had not done enough to explain this reality to the public. Kaya said that healthcare workers were among the lowest-paid public employees and that excessive workloads and duties imposed on them were causing serious burnout.




Kaya said, “There is a system that constantly directs people towards emergency departments and hospitals while undermining preventive healthcare,” and adding that health should be understood not merely in physical terms, but as a state of complete well-being encompassing housing, adequate nutrition, and mental, social and political well-being.




Kaya added: “While millions of people are waiting for services in hospitals, appointments are not being made on the grounds of insufficient funding. There is now a huge workforce of healthcare professionals waiting to be appointed. This situation is also contributing to exhaustion among healthcare workers.”




‘In Kartal on 29 November, in Ankara on 12 December’




Diren Can Kaya emphasised that healthcare was too vital a social issue to be left solely to healthcare workers and said that a joint struggle between those who provide healthcare and those who receive it was essential to securing free, high-quality and accessible healthcare services in people's mother tongues. Kaya said that they aimed to expand this struggle through people's assemblies and neighbourhood communes.




Kaya concluded with the following call: “We call on all employees, workers, young people and women to join the joint rallies in Kartal on 29 November and in Ankara on 12 December, organised at the call of the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DISK), the Confederation of Public Employees' Trade Unions (KESK), the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB) and the Turkish Medical Association (TTB), to demand our share of the budget and defend the people's right to quality healthcare.”

title: One family, six comrades
content:
Kurdish movements advocating the freedom of the Kurdish people and Kurdistan have been established in their dozens, from the period when the existence of the Kurds and Kurdistan was denied to the present day. Some of these movements carried out armed and political struggles for decades, while others disintegrated in their early years as a result of plots by their enemies. Many movements were established, but many were also eliminated. These movements carried out their activities through the love that the people of Kurdistan held in their hearts. Numerous young people sacrificed their lives for their objectives. Many Kurdish youths were tortured, imprisoned and killed for the same cause. Their fundamental aim was to struggle for a free Kurdistan. Thousands followed in their footsteps and embraced the ideology of Kurdistan's freedom. Among them were many people with distinctive and remarkable stories.




This article tells the life stories of comrades Nîştîman and Mezlûm and how they joined the struggle. Mezlûm and Nîştîman were life partners and comrades in struggle. They had two children and came from Mûçêj, a town in Kamyaran in Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat). They lived with strong patriotic convictions and devoted themselves to the struggle. Both had worked within organisations in Eastern Kurdistan and made sacrifices for their political activities.







 







Mezlûm Viyan described his disillusionment with Kurdish political movements and how he later became acquainted with the ideas of Abdullah Öcalan. He said: “My name is Mezlûm Viyan. I was born in Mûçêj, Kamyaran. Comrade Nîştîman and I had established a garden where we grew tomatoes. We had created a vegetable garden and dug a well there. One evening, while walking towards the village, I saw Öcalan's name written on the walls.




I had previously worked in other political movements. I was active in the Tudeh Party and later joined the Komala Party. I carried out political activities in Sine. Because of my activities, I also spent two years in Iranian prisons. However, these traditional parties betrayed the people. The good people among them were martyred. Others took control of these parties through conspiracies. After Kak Fuad was martyred, a family from Bokan took control of the Komala Party. This family put its own interests first and forgot the people. After witnessing all this, I came to hate politics. I would not allow anyone in our home to talk about politics because the people had been betrayed. Villagers had shared their food with them and opened their doors to them. Yet they went and surrendered, exposing our people to arrest. Many people were imprisoned as a result. From that day onwards, I hated politics. I would not allow anyone to discuss politics in my presence.”




Baz becomes the first to join the Freedom Movement




Mezlûm Viyan said that he embraced Abdullah Öcalan's ideas after reading his books. He said: “At one point, a cadre from the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) came to our home. I was told that he was a university student. That was how he was introduced to me. Later, one day at the university, I asked my son Baz, ‘Who is this Öcalan?’ He replied, ‘Would you like me to bring you his books?’ I said, ‘Bring them.’ He brought me the book How to Live. From its opening pages, I realised how different this leader's political definitions and ideas about building society were from those of Marx, Engels, Mao, Che Guevara, and even the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad Mustafa and all the books in the world. I do not know why, but my heart was racing as I read that book. The moment I sat beside the water pool and read it, I fell in love with that leader. As I read, I understood that his perspective on building society was different from other perspectives. I saw no personal interest in these ideas. That was why I fell in love with them.”




After becoming acquainted with the movement, Mezlûm's son Baz left his family and joined its ranks. Baz's decision marked the beginning of a remarkable story of patriotism for the family. Mezlûm Viyan said that Baz had travelled to the Qandil mountains, where he received ten days of training before returning to complete his university education. He recalled: “After university, Baz said, ‘I am going to join the movement.’ Baz was the first among us to join. After Baz joined, Nîştîman told me, ‘Go and ask about our son. Find out where he is and what he is doing.’ I left Eastern Kurdistan and travelled to Southern Kurdistan (Başûr). They told me to go to a valley called Qela Tukan. They said, ‘There are comrades in that valley.’ I hired a car and travelled to Qela Tukan. When the car stopped, several women comrades came to welcome me. They embraced me one by one and welcomed me. Then they took my hand and led me into a house.




I had never witnessed such beautiful conduct in society. Of course, people embrace one another, but I had never experienced an embrace as sincere as those of the comrades. The way they embraced mewas different and special. We were sitting inside. Directly opposite me sat a woman comrade with blue eyes and hair reaching down to her feet. I asked whether I could go outside to smoke a cigarette. She handed me an ashtray, tea and cigarettes. She asked, ‘Yabo, why have you come?’ The word ‘yabo’ has a slightly different meaning in Sorani, so I was a little confused. The woman comrade beside her explained, ‘She is using the word yabo to mean babo, or father.’ I replied, ‘My son has joined you. I have come to ask where he is and what he is doing.’ They asked me how long I had been there. I told them it had been 21 days. One comrade said, ‘I have not seen my family for 17 years.’ Another said, ‘I have not seen my family for ten years.’ A third said, ‘I have not seen my family for 14 years.’ If I remember correctly, that comrade was from Derik. She took my hand and said, ‘Yabo, consider me your own daughter. Here in these mountains, I am now in my own home.’




I told the comrades, ‘Call me a car. I am leaving.’ After the woman comrade spoke to me in that way, I felt ashamed to ask another question. Although the women comrades repeatedly asked me to stay that night, I said, ‘No, I am leaving.’ I got into the car and returned home. As I was climbing the stairs to our home, my elder son Pêywend was coming down. Nîştîman asked me, ‘Did you go? Did you see him?’ I replied, ‘Yes, I saw him. We met at two in the morning and greeted each other.’ I had been forced to lie. Pêywend said to me, ‘Do not lie to my mother.’ Newroz was approaching. We were told that families who visited the guerrilla areas during Newroz would be able to see their children. At that time, Pêywend was also involved in political activities. One night, I found a CD at home. When I watched it, I realised that it contained a speech by Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan). I understood that it belonged to Pêywend and that he too was involved in the activities. However, he was working secretly so that we would not know what he was doing.”




Elder son Pêywend joins the movement after his brother Baz




Mezlûm Viyan described how his elder son Pêywend joined the movement and how he and Nîştîman subsequently began their own activities. He said: “We went to the guerrilla areas for the Newroz celebrations. Pêywend had also come there. After we arrived, Pêywend said, ‘I am also joining the movement.’ Nîştîman told him, ‘May it bring good things.’ However, the comrades did not accept his decision. They told him, ‘Go and work in the cities.’ We had not been able to see Baz either. The comrades told us, ‘Come back on 4 April.’ We left and returned on 4 April. I asked a comrade where Baz was. He replied, ‘If you want to see Baz, you will have to walk for seven days.’ That evening, I went outside to smoke a cigarette and heard a voice. Someone was singing. The voice sounded like my son Baz's. I went inside and asked, ‘Why didn't you tell me the truth?’ He replied, ‘Why? What happened?’ I said, ‘Baz is singing outside.’ He laughed and said, ‘That's right. You will see Baz tomorrow.’ The following day, we went and Nîştîman saw Baz. Later, my elder son Pêywend also joined the movement, following his brother Baz.




We returned to Eastern Kurdistan. Nîştîman and I also began working. We carried out recruitment activities and distributed Leader Apo's books. Our nephew Helo lived with us. When he turned 20, we were eating together one day when he told me, ‘I am leaving tomorrow.’ After Baz and Pêywend, Helo also joined the movement. Nîştîman and I were left alone. Our tomato garden required a great deal of labour and many workers. When people living nearby heard that our children had joined the movement, they began gathering early in the morning to help in the garden. One morning, as Nîştîman and I were going to work, we saw around 100 people gathered in the garden. They had come to help us. They would not let us do any work. We only brought them food and water. So many people came to help that there was no work left for us to do.”




They are forced to move to Southern Kurdistan after the Rojava protests




Mezlûm described the demonstrations organised in solidarity with Kobanê and Rojava following attacks by Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) militants, as well as the Iranian state's attacks on protesters. He said: “During the uprisings in support of Rojava, a march and demonstration were planned for five in the afternoon. The day before the demonstration, two people working for the regime came to visit us. They said, ‘We are inviting you to this demonstration.’ I replied, ‘I am busy with my own work. I am a farmer and I have work to attend to.’ I told them we would not be coming. I said to Nîştîman, ‘Both my work and your organisational activities concern these people. If we go and take part in this demonstration, both of us will be eliminated.’ Those two people had not come to us for nothing. That evening, as we were walking along the street, Nîştîman said to me, ‘You are enjoying yourself, aren't you? Your children are putting their bodies in front of bullets, while you sit comfortably at home.’ After hearing those words, I made my decision and said, ‘All right, tomorrow we will take part in the demonstration too.’




I informed the young people around me and told them that we would join the demonstration the following day. Nîştîman and I set off for Sine. The street where the march was due to take place was filled with soldiers and police officers. I told Nîştîman, ‘This is not a march or demonstration. This is an operation to eliminate us.’ She replied, ‘Your mind always works negatively.’ When the young people taking part in the demonstration saw us, they said, ‘Look, comrade Mezlûm and comrade Nîştîman have joined the demonstration too.’ Everyone began applauding us and chanting ‘Bijî Kobanê’ (Long live Kobanê). Nîştîman and I moved to the front of the march. The street was overflowing with people. Demonstrations had begun throughout Sine. One young man was wearing a shirt over a T-shirt bearing the PKK flag. At that moment, the regime's police attacked him. I threw myself in front of him to prevent them from beating him. The police then attacked me. They broke two of my ribs and fractured my skull. At the same time, they were attacking Nîştîman with tear gas.




During the clashes, Nîştîman's bag went missing. I called her phone, but a young man answered. I asked who he was. He replied, ‘I have comrade Nîştîman's bag. Come and collect it.’ I thought Nîştîman had fallen into the hands of Iranian intelligence. However, there is a certain stubbornness in our family. So I said to myself, ‘Whatever happens, I am going.’ As I approached the place the young man had described, I called again. I saw Nîştîman's bag in the hands of a young man. He told me, ‘This is comrade Nîştîman's bag. Check whether anything inside is missing.’ As I was looking inside the bag, the young man said, ‘I know comrade Pêywend.’ I raised my head, but the young man was no longer there. Later, Nîştîman and I found each other again.”




Every sacrifice made their story more beautiful




Mezlûm Viyan concluded by describing their experience of displacement, the events following the uprising in support of Rojava, and how he and Nîştîman eventually joined the guerrilla ranks. He said: “After the demonstration, I received a phone call. I was told that Iranian intelligence had surrounded our home and that if we returned, we would certainly be arrested. We had no choice but to leave and move to Southern Kurdistan. After arriving, we stopped somewhere to drink tea. I said to Nîştîman, ‘Do you realise that the Iranian state has driven us from our land? They deliberately forced us out of our region. The Iranian state's policy is different. We did not leave of our own free will. We were exiled. They removed us so that nobody would remain in our region to carry out political and organisational activities.’




We stayed with the comrades for a while. We told them that we wanted to join the party, but they did not accept our request. We then went to Qeladizê and rented a house. We stayed there for some time. However, Viyan had remained in Eastern Kurdistan. He was also my nephew, my younger brother's son. I wanted Viyan to come here too. After travelling to Eastern Kurdistan, Viyan joined the movement of his own free will. We remained in Southern Kurdistan for a long time. I was constantly with the comrades, working alongside them. Nîştîman said to me, ‘Why are you so happy? You are always with the comrades, while I am always at home. Yes, we have established our organisation in our neighbourhood and formed communes with women, but these things are not enough.’ By then, the situation had deteriorated, and warplanes were bombing the areas where the comrades were based. Warplanes were flying over Qeladizê.




One day, I saw Nîştîman take the Kalashnikov-type weapon we had at home and climb onto the roof. She pointed the weapon towards the sky and began firing at the warplanes. On another occasion, I saw everyone we knew in Qeladizê take up their weapons and fire into the sky. Even Katyusha rockets and DShK heavy machine guns were used. People in Qeladizê were calling one another, saying, ‘A guerrilla mother has taken up her weapon and is firing into the sky.’ Then everyone began firing their weapons. Within minutes, Qeladizê had turned into something resembling hell. After this incident, Nîştîman also joined the movement. I joined after her. She went to take part in the activities of the women's movement, while I attended basic training for new fighters. That is how our family joined the movement.”




They were not in love with weapons or war. They were in love with an idea, and they followed that idea. They were devoted to the freedom of their homeland. They transformed their family ties into a story of national liberation. With every sacrifice they made, that story and their devotion grew stronger. Six comrades and resistance fighters emerged from one family. Nîştîman, Pêywend, Viyan, Helo and Helo Dersîm joined the ranks of the immortals at different times and in different areas of the struggle. They became an enduring example for those who remained and immortal monuments to courage.
