title: Çiğdem Doğu: Now is the time for women's self-defense
content:
Kurdistan Women's Communities (KJK) Executive Council member Çiğdem Doğu appeared on a special program broadcast by Medya Haber television, where she discussed the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated by Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan) and violence against women.




Part one of this lengthy interview can be read 

here

, and part two 

here

.




November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, emerged from the struggle of the Mirabal sisters, who paid a heavy price. Your movement and its approach to women's freedom also draw on these historical roots, enriching this legacy with their own values and carrying it to women in Turkey and Kurdistan. What should women do in this context? You frequently speak about self-defense. How can women develop their self-defense in biological, physical, psychological and social terms? What message would you like to send to women living in different cities, from Muş (Mûş) to Kayseri, Tekirdağ and Bolu, and from Amed to Mardin (Mêrdîn)?




We certainly want to address women throughout this entire geography. One of the fundamental dimensions of the Third World War is violence against women. It is extremely important to understand this as a whole, recognize the systemic nature of violence and identify its fundamental source. If we look at the figures concerning the killing of women, they reveal a toll comparable to that of a war. But when we look at the perpetrators, we encounter individual names. A woman's boyfriend, husband, father, brother, someone close to her or a schoolmate. Ahmet, Mehmet or someone else. The perpetrators are always presented as individuals. But this, too, is a form of concealment. Why has masculinity reached this point?




When discussing November 25, we frequently speak of the "women's question." However, the Kurdish People's Leader (Abdullah Öcalan) recently made an important observation: women themselves are not the problem. There is a male-dominated reality that turns women into a problem. There is a problem of dominant masculinity. We must approach November 25 and the struggle against violence from this perspective. There is a problem of masculinity that has become murderous. Of course, I am not speaking about all men. I am referring to those who commit such acts and those shaped by male-dominated culture. I want this distinction to be understood clearly. But did this problem of masculinity emerge on its own? People offer explanations such as "I was psychologically disturbed" or "I became extremely angry." Others claim that men have higher levels of certain hormones and that violence is therefore biological. But we are not animals. Human beings are human beings. Men are human, and women are human.




Human beings have the capacity to go beyond their hormonal and instinctive impulses. We possess analytical intelligence, emotions, morality and conscience. These qualities did not emerge without reason. They are what make us human, and this applies to men as well. Why, then, has violence reached a level comparable to warfare? There is a patriarchal system that produces this destructive social reality. Today, we call this the capitalist system. We mentioned Trump earlier. Trump is a particularly clear model and representative of the murderous, hierarchical, male-dominated personality. We can look at him to understand our era. Consider how very young girls, even children, have been brutally exploited. The person associated with this has now become the President of the United States. This reveals the nature of the system, its politics and its economy.




This is the source. Trump is one visible representative of those who operate this system, but there is also an invisible machinery behind it. That machinery continues to function. Men within society become involved in this system in different ways. As the system encourages male domination and gives men a share in that power, they become increasingly attached to it. The more attached they become, the more they look down on women and treat them as objects. They say, "She is my property." They say, "I cannot exist without her." Once a man sees a woman as his property, he believes he cannot exist without possessing her. This has created a terrifying contradiction and a deeply destructive culture. An enormous system of domination has been established through the ownership and objectification of women, particularly through control over women's bodies and sexuality. This is one of the main sources of violence.




Do television series, screenplays and films produced in Turkey also encourage this kind of masculinity? So many revolve around fathers and sons.




Television series in Turkey, Hollywood productions and even films described as science fiction largely reproduce masculinity and conventional femininity. Of course, there are some productions outside the system, and those should be considered separately. But the dominant pattern is the reproduction of traditional gender roles.




Consider Turkish television series. I recently saw a scene in a film. If I were in the position of women's movements in Turkey, I would file a formal complaint. Mothers, fathers, women's organizations and even children should have complained about it because of the harmful example it presented. It was a scene of extreme violence. A man picked up a chainsaw and was about to kill someone. The scene presented this with laughter, almost as though it were something admirable.




They seem to portray this as the behavior of a brave man. 




How can that be considered bravery? I am giving one example, but there are many others. Men become accustomed to this violence. Women become accustomed to it. Children watch it and become accustomed to it. Recently, a man in Afyon traveled from village to village and killed eight people within six hours. There have also been incidents in Turkey involving children who took weapons to schools and killed other children and adults. Violence is being directed not only against women but against society as a whole. We must question its source.




There are also factors in Turkey that are fueled by war and an atmosphere of hostility. When examining violence against women, we must discuss these issues seriously. We must also confront the patriarchal and fascist culture that produces such violence.




Violence in digital media has reached truly alarming levels. There are women driven to suicide. Women are constantly told how they should look: how their eyebrows, eyes and hair should appear, and what kind of beauty they must achieve. If they cannot meet these expectations, some experience severe psychological distress and may be driven toward suicide. These are terrible realities, and they are also forms of violence. Women are placed under enormous pressure. There are also cases in which women are manipulated into compromising situations, photographed and then threatened or blackmailed with those images. They are told, "I will tell your family," or threatened with exposure to others. Through these methods, women are forced into submission and pushed toward prostitution, informant activities or drugs. Whichever way we look at it, an extraordinary atmosphere of violence is being created. We must put an end to this. Our protests must also clearly identify the source of the problem.




If you remember, before the coronavirus pandemic, women's movements around the world had developed powerful protests, including that famous dance. They were pointing directly at the state. They had correctly identified the source of the problem. Women were pointing to the capitalist system. Then the coronavirus pandemic began. Society became completely isolated. For nearly two years, a strategy was pursued that disrupted the radicalism and organized character of the struggle and separated people from one another. It was not simply a disease. The pandemic also created political disengagement. These developments cannot be considered independently of one another. We must identify those responsible and demand accountability. This is extremely important. Of course, when someone commits murder, we must demand accountability from that person. But there is also a fundamental source. There is the nation-state, industrialism, capital and, in the case of Kurdistan, colonialism. There is a system that denies your existence. All these factors produce violence within masculinity. We must take a clear position against them.




'Women must create their own aesthetic and moral values'




These are what we might call our negative responsibilities: struggling against destructive forces. But we also have positive responsibilities, responsibilities of construction. What must we build? Suppose I seek justice through the state's courts and the perpetrator is punished. Can that alone protect me? I remain vulnerable in every aspect of life. For example, I have no economic independence and have been condemned to poverty. I face threats whenever I walk through the streets. How am I supposed to defend myself?




Women's bodies are under attack from every direction. They have been fragmented and objectified. There is an assault on women through imposed standards of beauty. Two of the world's most profitable industries are the arms industry and the beauty and cosmetics industry. An enormous market has been created. Why? So that women will make themselves attractive to men. This is terrible. My health is threatened by this system. There are countless cosmetic procedures, beauty products and other practices, creating further markets. Women are reduced entirely to objects. This, too, is a form of violence.




Women must establish their own standards of life, morality and aesthetics. They must determine the principles of a free life for themselves. Do I currently have the means to defend myself in this respect? No. 




Who is most deprived of education? Women. How can I educate myself and establish my own way of life without becoming dependent on the state or dominant men? The same questions apply to economic life, education and healthcare.




Art is also extremely important. How can we create a new culture of free womanhood? We have a form of masculinity deeply immersed in violence. What would a new, free masculinity look like? Art should explore this. For example, art developed under women's leadership could examine what an ideal man or an ideal woman should be. How should democracy, equality and freedom be expressed in relationships between women and men? Why should we not create these ideals through literature, theatre and cinema?We already know that violence against women exists. Simply repeating that fact tells us nothing new. We must focus on how to overcome this violence. I believe artistic activities can contribute a great deal. The struggle against violence toward women must also have an artistic dimension. There is also the question of how I can defend myself physically. These are areas we must develop. For example, we can establish communes. We can create healthcare communes, communes concerned with aesthetics and morality, and spaces where we develop our own standards and values. We can establish communes based on equality. We can create democratic family communes by questioning the existing structure of the family and organizing against violence.




'

Women must respond to attacks from wherever they come'




Notice how people around the world constantly say that "the right is rising." As I mentioned earlier, this is also part of an effort to shape perceptions. What provides the foundation for this narrative? The traditional family structure. Women are assigned conventional duties, while men are expected to fulfill traditional masculine roles. This is constantly imposed on society. What would alternative relationships between women and men look like? How can we develop an ideal model? Why should communes not be established around these questions? In my view, each of these constitutes a fundamental component of self-defense. But there is also the question of physical violence. How can a woman defend herself when she is directly attacked? We encounter truly horrific examples. Every time we see them, we are deeply affected. A woman is attacked in the street with a gun or knife, or she is beaten. She is often unable to do anything because she has been left defenseless. Why should women not develop their skills in martial arts and close-combat sports?




Self-defense does not necessarily mean taking up a weapon and fighting. The law itself recognizes the right to legitimate self-defense in certain circumstances. If you face a deadly attack, you have the right to defend yourself within the bounds of legitimate self-defense. But when you face any form of attack, wherever it comes from, you must respond. You should not simply defend yourself. You must also strike back so that the attacker cannot continue. You must become a deterrent force. I am speaking here at the individual level. But I also believe that young women, in particular, can establish their own self-defense groups. They can defend one another in their neighborhoods and cities. If one woman is attacked, the others should come together to defend her. They should respond collectively, as a commune. Rather than remaining in such a helpless position, we must be able to demand accountability. If they strike a woman once, we should strike back ten times. Women themselves should strike back ten times. At the same time, if we build the forms of organization I mentioned earlier, through which women can create their own free lives, establish academies and communes, and make their own decisions, I believe this will be what truly prevents violence and gradually eliminates it.




'Now is the time for women's self-defense'




November 25 is approaching. As the Kurdistan Women's Communities, we attach particular importance to this date. We should not limit our activities to a single day. They can continue for weeks, ten days or an entire month. We should establish such a culture. Of course, the struggle is continuous, but November can be a period of particular focus on combating violence against women. We can organize educational activities and protests. We should commemorate women individually, remembering each by name. We must keep alive the memory of every woman murdered by the male-dominated system. We should discuss our strategies of struggle and organize educational activities. The name of our campaign as the Kurdistan Women's Communities is "Now Is the Time for Women." This November is our time. Now is the time for women. Now is the time for women's self-defense. Now is the time to build a free life for women. Now is the time to demand accountability for the violence produced by the male-dominated system.




We should approach November, particularly November 25, with this perspective and organize powerful actions and activities. I want to emphasize this especially to Kurdish women and to women throughout Turkey. When we speak of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, our women comrades and friends from Turkey are extremely valuable to us. Building this fundamental alliance and developing the struggle for peace on that basis are extremely important. But we must also develop a powerful period of action involving women throughout the Middle East and across the world. We must strengthen our position and intensify our struggle against male domination.

title: Eleven years ago, the liberation of Shengal
content:
When ISIS mercenaries stood at the doors of the Yazidi town of Shengal in north-west Iraq, thousands of Peshmerga and Asayish (Local Security Force) of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), who until that very moment controlled the town, made a quick getaway without shooting even one single bullet. As a result of the flight of the KDP Peshmerga, thousands of Yazidis were slaughtered by ISIS, thousands more were abducted, predominantly women and children, and sold at markets into slavery. Interestingly, shortly before the genocide took place, the KDP forces seized all the arms and weapons the Yazidis had at that time and took into custody three of the twelve guerrillas of the People's Defense Forces (HPG) and the Free Women's Troops (YJA-Star), who came to the rescue of the fleeing Yazidi people. All this made it indeed very clear how well-prepared and organized this extensive genocide actually was.




Only with the help of a dozen guerrilla fighters from the PKK were hundreds of thousands of people saved from certain death or enslavement. Reinforcements from the HPG and YJA Star then moved out of the Kurdistan mountains. Together with the YPG (People’s Defense Units) and YPJ (Women’s Defense Units), a corridor of escape to Rojava was created. Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Shengal Women's Units (YJŞ) were formed, and the region was liberated step by step. In January 2015, an autonomous council was proclaimed. On 31 October 2015, an offensive began to liberate the villages in the west of the city of Shengal, and on 13 November 2015, ISIS was completely driven out of the region.




3 August genocide in Shengal




The Islamic State (ISIS) killed, captured and displaced all 400,000 Yazidi people living in Shengal on 3 August 2014, in a genocide that disproportionately affected children. About 10,000 Yazidis were killed or abducted. Half of all those executed were children, according to a report by multi-national researchers in the journal PLoS Medicine.




Nearly all (93%) of those who eventually died on Mount Shengal from injuries or lack of food and water were also children. Of the around 6,400 abducted Yazidis, it’s estimated about half were children, according to the Yazidi-led nonprofit Nadia’s Initiative. Boys as young as seven were sent to ISIS training camps and girls as young as nine were subjected to rape and sexual enslavement, according to a Save the Children report.




While over three thousand Yazidi citizens abducted by ISIS have been rescued, there is still no news from as many Yazidis abducted by ISIS during the genocidal onslaught. Many families are still waiting to learn the fate of their loved ones.




More than twelve years after the genocide committed by ISIS, efforts to exhume and identify the victims continue. According to Iraq’s Martyrs Foundation, 90 mass graves have been discovered so far. Of these, 85 have been fully excavated, with the recovery of human remains and documentation completed. In total, the remains of around 700 people have been recovered.




The Iraqi Martyrs Foundation also established a specialized unit to assist victims’ relatives. Psychologists and social workers are expected to support families receiving the remains of their murdered loved ones after years of uncertainty.




Turkish attacks after the ISIS genocide




Shengal is the last remaining settlement area of the Yazidi community. Starting from 2017, the region was frequently bombed by Turkish fighter jets and drones. The specific targets were mostly facilities of the administrative body ‘Democratic Autonomous Council of Shengal’ (MXDŞ) or the self-defence units. Many of the fatalities were civilians, often survivors of the ISIS genocide of 2014. Many militants of the PKK movement who took part in the fight against ISIS in Shengal and protected the Yazidi community were also killed in attacks by the Turkish state.




Democratic integration process in Shengal




Following the genocide, the reconstruction of Shengal continues. People's Councils have been established in the region, and the Yazidi women’s movement is a driving force in the struggle for self-determination and survival.




On 26 October,

 

the YBŞ and YJŞ confirmed their agreement with the Iraqi government to integrate a total of 4,165 fighters into the state security forces.




At a ceremony in the Shengal Mountains, the two forces stated that the success of the agreement would depend on whether the rights of the Yazidi population were protected, the consequences of the genocide were addressed, and the agreed commitments were fulfilled.




In their joint statement, the YBŞ and YJŞ confirmed that they had reached an agreement with Baghdad to end their independent military status. Their forces will operate within Iraqi security institutions in the future. Control over their weapons will also be transferred to the state in accordance with the agreed arrangements. The decision was made out of a sense of responsibility for Shengal’s security and in recognition of Iraq’s territorial integrity.




At the same time, the YBŞ and YJŞ emphasized that their integration was subject to clear commitments: “The prerequisite is that the agreed provisions are implemented, the rights of our male and female fighters are upheld, the dignity of our fallen fighters is protected, and the security of Shengal, as well as the rights and autonomy of its people, are guaranteed.”




For the YBŞ and YJŞ, the military agreement represents only one part of the necessary steps. They are calling for the fate of Yazidis who have been missing since the genocide to be clarified and for justice to be delivered to the victims’ families. They also emphasize the need to create conditions for the return of displaced people and to advance the reconstruction of Shengal.




The units are also demanding the strengthening of civilian institutions and local self-governance. Accordingly, all communities in Shengal must be involved in political decision-making. Only in this way, they say, can a democratic system be established that serves the interests of the entire population.




In their statement, the YBŞ and YJŞ thanked the Iraqi government and all those who have supported the Yazidis since the genocide. They called for this cooperation to continue during the practical implementation of the agreement.

title: DEM Party emphasises priority tasks of new period
content:
The DEM Party Council began its second meeting following the congress by commemorating Tuncer Sağlam and Nesrin Aslan.




According to the final statement, the meeting included a comprehensive assessment of political, economic and social developments in Turkey, the Middle East and the world.




The statement said that, guided by the political vision set out at the congress and an awareness of its historical responsibilities, the Council had reached the following conclusions in order to determine the course of struggle for the period ahead:




Solidarity is our fundamental principle




1. The world is going through a period in which people's aspirations for peace, equality, freedom and democracy are confronting governments' policies of war, violence and hegemony. In response to the poverty, unemployment and inequality deepened by the capitalist system, youth, labour and popular movements stretching from France to Serbia and from Latin America to Europe are demonstrating the possibilities of a democratic and egalitarian way of life. Solidarity with struggles against exploitation, oppression, discrimination and lawlessness is our fundamental principle.




In the Middle East, policies of war directed against Iran, conflicts extending from Palestine to Lebanon and from Syria to Yemen, and efforts to establish regional alliances threaten the will and democratic future of the peoples of the region. Rather than becoming part of these policies, Turkey should assume responsibility for regional peace, equality among peoples and democratic solutions. We oppose the government's orientation towards the Mecca Pact, the Badr Agreement and its new relationships with regional powers, as these carry the risk of aligning Turkey with policies of war and hegemony.




The future of a multilingual, multi-faith and multicultural Middle East cannot be built through military alliances and sectarian policies, but through the equality and free will of its peoples. Recognition of the national, cultural and democratic rights of all peoples in the region is indispensable.




Kurda must come together on common ground




2. Overcoming political divisions within the Kurdistan Regional Government and bringing Kurdish political forces together is of historic importance for the unity of the Kurdish people, their shared future and the protection of their achievements. Political differences must not be allowed to weaken the people's collective will. We call on all Kurdish political forces to overcome their divisions through dialogue and come together on common ground for the unity of the Kurdish people.




Political and legal steps must be taken in the second phase of the process




3. The Peace and Democratic Society Process represents a historic opportunity for Turkey's democratic future. For developments aimed at ending conflict and violence as methods of resolving disputes to lead to lasting peace, democratic political channels must be expanded and all sections of society must be able to participate. The process concerns the shared future of society as a whole, not merely the parties involved, and also places responsibility on pro-democracy forces.




Political and legal steps for the second phase must be taken without delay. It is essential to implement the requirements of the legislation adopted by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey (TBMM), establish legal safeguards suited to the needs of the process, and resolve fundamental issues, particularly the right to hope and the status of Mr Abdullah Öcalan.




Ending the appointment of trustees in place of elected local authorities, recognising the will of the people, implementing the rulings of the Constitutional Court (AYM) and the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), and guaranteeing the life and health rights of sick prisoners are indispensable requirements for democratisation.




Peace is not simply the silencing of weapons; it means confronting the truth, establishing equal citizenship, securing rights and freedoms, ensuring justice and building a democratic society. A democratic and peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question is one of the fundamental conditions for Turkey's transformation into a democratic and social republic. Our party remains determined to maintain its constructive and responsible approach in order to ensure the success of this historic opportunity.




Democratic forces must preserve platforms for joint struggle




4. Joint action by pro-democracy forces in Turkey has become even more important in the face of attempts to fragment the opposition. Our fundamental orientation is to bring left-wing, socialist, democratic and progressive forces together around shared democratic goals while respecting their differences; and to ensure that the struggle for democracy is not confined to political institutions but becomes a collective struggle involving every section of society.




Preserving and developing platforms for joint struggle is one of the priority tasks of this period.




Inflation, high cost of living, unemployment and poverty worsen people's living conditions




5. While inflation, the high cost of living, unemployment and poverty are worsening people's living conditions, the government's economic policies continue to protect the interests of business and capital. The plundering of public resources and the networks of political influence exposed by the fund scandal have demonstrated the injustice of this system. Those truly responsible must be exposed, and the people must not be made to shoulder additional taxes and economic burdens.




Our demand in opposition to the 2027 budget, which disregards workers, labourers, women, young people and pensioners, is clear: the budget must be for the people, not for war and capital.




In this context, our Bread, Peace and Justice campaign must be taken into workers' homes, fields, schools, hospitals and all areas of production. Strengthening our relations with labour and professional organisations, and bringing together the demands of workers, pensioners, farmers and impoverished sections of society within a common struggle, are among our priorities.




Organised struggle is essential to securing workers' rights, a dignified life and social justice.




Women's struggle, young people and ecology




6. Women's struggle for equality and freedom against male domination and capitalist exploitation is decisive in building a democratic society. The struggle against male and state violence against women, economic and social inequalities, and discrimination against women with disabilities will develop through the will and organised strength of women, who are founding actors in the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Joint action with women's movements as part of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November provides an important platform for making the demand for a life free from violence, exploitation and inequality a broader social cause.




Solidarity with young people's struggles against poverty, unemployment and a lack of prospects, and the expansion of spaces in which young people can express their own views, exercise their will and develop their organised strength, are among our fundamental responsibilities.




Developing relations with all sections of youth, from university students to young workers, unemployed young people and young women, as well as strengthening youth organisations in every province and district, are priorities.




We stand alongside struggles that defend life against ecological destruction and the transformation of nature into a sphere for capital accumulation. During the COP31 process, the real causes of the ecological crisis and the profit-driven policies of corporations must be exposed.




It is important to bring together the struggles stretching from the Kaz Mountains to Cudi, from Akbelen to Varto and Ordu Çobantepe; to give strong organisational support to the People's Climate Summit and to the We Defend Life demonstration to be held in Antalya on 14 November.




Organisational renewal and a new initiative




7. Our Party Council considers organisational renewal and a new initiative essential in response to the needs of the new period.




Overcoming shortcomings, strengthening social ties and our capacity for struggle, establishing a culture of collective work, and reaching new sections of society are the foundations of this renewal.




An organisational approach based on democratic participation from the local level to the centre, establishing direct relationships with the people, and ensuring the active participation of women and young people must take root in every sphere of life, from neighbourhoods and workplaces to areas of labour and universities.




The goals of a democratic republic, radical democracy and a democratic society require strengthening society's own capacity for self-organisation, unity among pro-democracy forces, and the transformation of the collective will of the peoples into political power.




Alliance politics must be developed through a perspective of joint struggle and social transformation, rather than being restricted to election periods.




Overcoming organizational limitations and shortcomings




The statement concluded: “Our Party Council has identified the tasks of the new period in line with our party's historical responsibilities and the expectations of our peoples.




Bringing our political aspirations together with social struggle, overcoming our organisational limitations and shortcomings, strengthening our ties with the peoples, and developing a shared will for joint struggle are the fundamental responsibilities of this period.




The social forces and accumulated experience of struggle needed to build this future already exist. The task now is to unite this strength, organise it and turn it into the leading driving force of democratic transformation.




Together with all our organisations, elected representatives and comrades in struggle, we will advance our struggle for peace, democracy, freedom and social justice.”

title: Ayşe Berktay: Women's direct participation is essential to peace
content:
Writer Ayşe Berktay, who participated in peace initiatives organized by women during previous resolution processes and met with women in many cities, spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the role women should play in it.




Ayşe Berktay recalled the work carried out by women's movements during the 2013–2015 resolution process, stressing that women should not merely support peace but must also be directly involved in decision-making mechanisms.




Ayşe Berktay emphasized the importance of building social support for peace, stating that the process cannot be reduced to negotiations between political actors. She stressed that the Kurdish freedom movement, particularly women, would not allow such an approach and said that women's organized will must be brought to the forefront to achieve a democratic solution.




'Women must participate as decision-makers at every stage of peace processes'




Ayşe Berktay stated that the 2013–2015 resolution process did not begin suddenly and should be understood as part of the search for a political solution to the Kurdish question that emerged in 2009.




She said that efforts to achieve peace could be traced further back to 2005 and even 1993, highlighting the importance of joint work between the Kurdish women's movement and feminist and socialist women from Turkey.




Ayşe Berktay said: "It is both possible and necessary to trace the process that emerged in July 2009 under the name 'Democratic Opening' further back to 2005 and, when viewed as a whole, as far back as 1993.




In the years around 2009, as the possibility of peace began to be felt, both the Kurdish women's movement and socialist and feminist women's movements in Turkey began coming together, holding discussions and organizing in solidarity against repression to spread the message, aspiration and language of peace.




The Democratic Free Women's Movement (DÖKH) inviting a large group of women to Amed (Diyarbakır) for discussions was critical in this regard. Ankara followed, then Berçelan-Taksim and the Peace Points. The Women's Initiative for Peace (BIKG) emerged from these joint efforts.




The Democratic Free Women's Movement was important in establishing a more structured platform for feminist and socialist women to meet, discuss, build relationships and work together.




These preparations formed the foundation and background for the activities carried out during the 2013–2015 process. Women examined peace experiences around the world and shared their findings with the public. The relationship between violence against women, militarism and war was addressed.




The need for women to participate as equal decision-makers at every stage of the peace process was constantly kept on the agenda. Women established various commissions and produced reports, activities and materials concerning different aspects of the process.




Following the Paris Massacre, there was a powerful collective commitment both to Sara, Rojbîn and Ronahî (Sakine Cansız, Fidan Doğan and Leyla Şaylemez, the three Kurdish women activists assassinated in Paris on 9 January 2013) and, through them, to the resolution process itself.”




'The importance of women's work became evident a decade ago'




Ayşe Berktay recalled that a woman representing the Kurdish women's movement joined the delegation when visits to Imralı began. She also stated that women from Turkey established the Women's Freedom Assembly (KÖM) to develop their collective voice and will.




Ayşe Berktay said that women's organizations prepared reports on the peace process through the commissions they established and carried out activities in different cities.




She said: "Efforts were made to establish an organized structure capable of bringing women's collective will to the negotiating table through commissions and reports. Throughout this process, both the Women's Initiative for Peace and the Women's Freedom Assembly worked tirelessly.




Women carried out work through monitoring commissions and truth commissions in Lice, Varto, Dersim, Suruç and along the Kobanê border. The importance and urgency of expanding this work became evident."




'

Women must participate in decision-making mechanisms'




Ayşe Berktay stated that raising the demand for peace and supporting the process were important but insufficient on their own. She stressed that women must participate directly in discussions about how peace will be built and in the mechanisms where decisions are made.




She emphasized that women's participation in decision-making processes must be based not only on representatives but also on their organized collective will.




Ayşe Berktay said: "If the solution is to be democratic, it is essential that women, who have contributed this labor and, beyond that, who build and reproduce life and constitute the stem cells of social existence, participate directly as actors in discussions and decisions about how the process will unfold.




This is an indispensable condition for the process to be democratic and to have a real impact on people's lives. But the question of how that direct participation will take place is also decisive.




The participation of a few women experts alone cannot bring about change or ensure that society becomes part of this process. Women as a social force must mobilize and make their collective will visible as an undeniable presence.




Making this will visible is itself a form of organization. Those who attend the meetings will carry that collective will into them."




'We are in a process where everything must move forward together'




Ayşe Berktay stated that one of the main tasks facing the women's movement is to establish strong relationships with society and make peace part of everyday life. She said that the process cannot be carried forward solely through legal and technical arrangements.




Ayşe Berktay emphasized that everyone must expand their work in their own field, engage with society and take steps to ensure that the peace process finds a place in everyday life. She highlighted the importance of the women's movement establishing a broad network of social relationships.




Ayşe Berktay continued: "We need to establish genuinely democratic and equal relationships with the people around us, share our experiences, joys and difficulties, make sense of them together and find solutions.




We must understand that we are not dealing with a technical issue. Of course, there are technical dimensions to the matter. They are necessary and important, and they will certainly be addressed. Women will also play their part in this.




But as far as I can see, what the women's movement must focus on and mobilize around is creating a broad network of relationships, a foundation rooted in everyday life that can produce solutions and open new paths.




What matters most is being able to embark on this path together with society. This also requires knowing and understanding not only our own historical sociology but also that of other peoples and social groups. It requires depth.




We are in a process where everything must move forward together. On the one hand, there are legal matters and commissions; on the other, the transformation of mindsets and relationships. If we lose sight of this compass, we will not succeed.




We need to understand and define the task before us properly, and then pursue it. We must be constructive, creative and capable of opening new paths.




When women take ownership of a task and pursue it, they can actually bring the whole of society along with them. The key is whether we can succeed in mobilizing women as a social force."




'The process cannot be reduced to negotiations between political actors'




Ayşe Berktay stressed that the Peace and Democratic Society Process cannot be limited to negotiations between political actors, stating that becoming a genuine political subject requires building social power and an organized collective will.




She said that participation in decision-making mechanisms is important, but collective struggle is also necessary to ensure that decisions are implemented, monitored and that emerging problems are resolved.




Ayşe Berktay concluded: "Being a genuine subject in this process is about becoming a social force, a collective will. Because being a subject is not something that can be achieved simply by attending a meeting where decisions are made. It also involves ensuring that those decisions are implemented, monitoring them, resolving problems, expressing a collective will, acting together to fulfill its requirements and following through."




Who is Ayşe Berktay?




Ayşe Berktay is a writer, translator, women's rights advocate and peace activist.




Ayşe Berktay studied at the Faculty of Architecture at Middle East Technical University (METU) and went abroad following the military coup of 12 September 1980. After returning to Turkey in the 1990s, she became involved in the women's movement, anti-war activism and peace initiatives.




Ayşe Berktay also served as a member of the Party Assembly of the Peace and Democracy Party (BDP). She was arrested in 2011 as part of an investigation into the Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) and spent 27 months in prison. She was released on 20 December 2013 pending trial.




During the 2013–2015 resolution process, Ayşe Berktay worked particularly on women's equal and direct participation in peace negotiations, building social support for peace and resolving the Kurdish question through democratic means.




Through her involvement in the Women's Initiative for Peace, she helped bring together women from different political backgrounds and social groups around the demand for peace.




Ayşe Berktay received the PEN/Barbara Goldsmith Freedom to Write Award in 2013.

title: YPJ spokesperson Ruksen Mihemed: We can only achieve our freedom through our own struggle
content:
What does self-defense mean for women whose identity, history and social existence have been subjected to attacks for generations? And what conditions must be established to ensure that women no longer have to depend on others to make decisions about their security, their rights and their future?




According to Ruksen Mihemed, spokesperson for the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) in Rojava, these questions lie at the heart of a struggle that extends far beyond armed resistance.




In an interview with ANF, Mihemed reflected on 15 years of women’s organizing and self-defense in Northeast Syria. She discusses the establishment of the YPJ, the experiences of the women’s revolution and the challenges arising from the ongoing restructuring of Syria.




“When a woman defends herself, there is life. But if she entrusts her defense to others, she cannot protect her life. The consequence is death,” Mihemed said.










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/7e263871_20261110221245_2026-11-10-qamislo-ruksen-mihemed-ypj-komutani-jpj-ve-25-kasim_1.mp4










Self-defense begins with awareness of one’s own identity




The emergence of independent women’s defense structures was closely linked to the social organizing that developed during the Rojava Revolution. Women began establishing their own institutions, taking responsibility in political decision-making processes and organizing independently in the field of defense.




“With the Rojava Revolution, women began to organize, and their participation in defense became a necessity. But first, women had to recognize their own identity and existence, learn about their history, understand themselves and develop an awareness of self-defense,” the YPJ spokesperson said.




She continued: “Our fundamental principle was that women should gain confidence in themselves, be able to express their thoughts freely and make their own decisions. On this foundation, they subsequently became increasingly involved in the field of defense.”




YPJ wrote a new chapter in the history of women’s struggle




With the formation of the YPJ, an independent women’s military organization emerged within the Kurdish freedom movement in Rojava. Its development was part of a broader social process in which women established their own political and institutional structures.




“With its establishment, the YPJ also wrote a new chapter in history: the history of a new women’s struggle. For the first time, an autonomous women’s force was established. This gave women the opportunity to create their own representation in all areas,” Mihemed noted.




“If self-defense has no place in a woman’s life, neither her rights, her legal status nor her life are protected. This is precisely where the YPJ took action. It created a system intended to ensure security, dignity and a life free from violence.”




Mihemed also emphasized the international impact of the YPJ: “Over these 15 years, the YPJ’s struggle has brought together not only women in Rojava and the Middle East, but also women around the world under a common banner of struggle. It has helped foster a shared stance and a spirit of solidarity among women.”




Women’s rights as a point of contention in Syria’s restructuring




As negotiations continue over Syria’s political and institutional future, questions are also emerging about the preservation of the women’s structures established in Northeast Syria over the past several years. Mihemed directed her criticism particularly at the Syrian transitional government, saying: “Damascus is still not convinced that the women’s question and women’s freedom are fundamental issues. It has failed to recognize that no country can be built without women’s organizing and that lasting stability in the fields of defense and security is impossible without their participation. Instead, a male-dominated mentality continues to prevail.”




According to the YPJ spokesperson, negotiations over the country’s future political system are therefore inseparably linked to women’s legal status: “This mentality must change. We must not forget that injustice committed against women is also an injustice against society as a whole. Women’s political and legal rights must be guaranteed within the emerging system.”




‘Appointing a few women to official positions does not mean recognizing women’s will’




Mihemed drew a distinction between the participation of individual women in state institutions and the recognition of autonomous women’s structures: “Recognizing women means recognizing their own system and their will. Giving a few women positions in certain areas does not necessarily mean that women’s will is being accepted. Fundamental changes and concrete steps are needed here.”




This demand also shapes the YPJ’s position in the ongoing negotiations over its future status within Syria’s security structures. The Women’s Protection Units insist on maintaining an autonomous organizational structure and on the direct participation of their command structure in the talks.




YPJ demands direct dialogue instead of negotiations through intermediaries




As previously reported, an agreement was reached to recognize two autonomous YPJ battalions as special forces units, each comprising 400 female fighters. In addition, the YPJ submitted the personnel records of 1,484 members of their structures. However, the practical implementation of the agreement remains pending.




Another point of contention concerns the format of the negotiations. Mihemed noted that talks have so far taken place exclusively through intermediaries.




“These steps are being taken through intermediaries. No direct dialogue has yet been established with our female commanders. We are convinced that the steps already initiated would progress more quickly and lead to clearer results if discussions were held directly with our commanders. The absence of direct dialogue is a significant shortcoming and, at the same time, reflects a particular mentality. The right approach is to speak directly with the parties involved.”




This century is the century of women




Reflecting on the current situation, Mihemed issueed an appeal to women both inside and outside Rojava: “Today, the system built by women is facing numerous attacks. That is why we, as women, must not retreat from our struggle, wherever we may be. This century is the century of women. From now on, we will shape our own lives. We can only achieve our freedom through our own struggle.”




According to Mihemed, securing the political and legal foundations of the changes achieved so far remains a task for women’s organizations.




“We must make our position clear against every form of paternalism and must never make concessions along our path. We will continue to defend the gains we have fought for, protected and sustained through tremendous effort, and we will secure them through constitutional and political guarantees.”




‘The struggle against violence must be waged every day’




Mihemed also commented on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25. On this occasion, she called for continuous organizing against patriarchal violence: “November 25 is a day when a particularly determined stance is taken against violence against women. But the struggle against attacks, violence and paternalism must not be confined to November 25. It is a struggle that must be waged every day.”

title: “Shared Stories, Free Cinema”: 6th Rojava Film Festival opens on Friday
content:
The 6th International Rojava Film Festival will open on Friday, November 13, with the screening of “Heval Kekê Min” by Haşim Aydemir. Under the theme “Çîrokên Hevpar, Sînemaya Azad” (Shared Stories, Free Cinema), the festival will bring filmmakers from various countries together with audiences in Rojava through November 20. Alongside feature films and documentaries, the program includes discussions on the social significance of cinema, collective filmmaking and the conditions for independent cultural production.




The main venue will be the Mihemed Şêxo Center in Qamişlo, where the film screenings will take place. Workshops, expert discussions and panel discussions will be held at the TEV-ÇAND, Sine Jin and Hunergeha Welat cultural centers. A special focus will be the “Ji Rojava” (From Rojava) section, featuring five productions from the region. The program will also include Kurdish-language short films, international feature films and documentaries.




Opening with music, dance and “Heval Kekê Min”




Friday’s opening ceremony will begin at 5:00 p.m. at the Mihemed Şêxo Center. MA Music will provide the musical program, while Narin Dance will present a dance performance. At 7:00 p.m., the opening film “Heval Kekê Min,” directed by Haşim Aydemir, will be screened.




The accompanying program of professional events will begin on Saturday, November 14. From 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. at Sine Jin, documentary filmmaker and editor Sasha Ayoub will introduce the work of Stories Film Lab. The program supports independent filmmakers in Syria in developing their projects. Films produced through the lab will also be screened during the event.




Film screenings will begin at 11:00 a.m. with “The Country Judge.” Other selections include the Kurdish-language short films “House of the Moon” and “Dorpêç,” as well as the documentary “The Wedding of the Pirs.”




From 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. at TEV-ÇAND, cinematographer Cemil Kızıldağ will lead a workshop on the visual language of cinema. The session will explore the creative possibilities of visual composition and cinematic storytelling.




Filmmaking practice and stories from Rojava




On Sunday, November 15, two multi-day workshops will begin. Cinematographer and lighting designer Jafar Amin Al-Betar will provide theoretical foundations and practical training in film lighting at Hunergeha Welat from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. The workshop will continue on November 16 and 17. Meanwhile, documentary filmmaker Guevara Namer will lead a workshop at Sine Jin focusing on the documentary filmmaking process and her experiences in international film production. The second part of her workshop will take place on November 16.




The “Ji Rojava” section will also begin that day. “Rêwiyên Ser Riya Agir” will be screened at 11:00 a.m., followed by “Keziyên Berxwedanê” at 11:50 a.m.




At 3:00 p.m., director Sêvînaz Evdikê, known for her film “Berbû,” will introduce the Nûjîyan Women’s Film Festival at TEV-ÇAND. At the same time, the documentary “Kî me ez?” will be screened at the Mihemed Şêxo Center.




The evening program will feature two more documentaries: “04.17 Adıyaman” at 6:00 p.m., followed by “Pêlên Kurdan” at 7:10 p.m. Both screenings will be followed by discussions with the audience.




Ten years of collective filmmaking in Rojava




On Monday, November 16, the experiences of the Rojava Film Commune will take center stage alongside the film screenings. “To Fetch a Pail of Water” will be screened at 11:00 a.m., followed by the documentary “Under the Flags the Sun” at 3:00 p.m.




From 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m., a panel discussion on the collective filmmaking practices of the Rojava Film Commune will take place at TEV-ÇAND. Since its establishment in 2015, the commune has been developing collectively organized approaches to filmmaking.




Moderated by Mirzan Bekir, the discussion will bring together founding members Diyar Hesso and Şêro Hindê and sound designer Coni Docolomansky, who worked on the films “Kobanê” and “Berbû.” The discussion will focus on experiences with collective production processes and the development of an independent filmmaking practice in Rojava.




Screenwriting and the Kurdish Question in Cinema




On Tuesday, November 17, screenwriter Önder Çakar will lead a workshop on developing film protagonists at Sine Jin from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. The workshop will explore the process of developing a character from an initial concept to its full realization in a screenplay.




The “Ji Rojava” series will continue with “Youthful Wrinkle” at 12:00 p.m. and “Nameya Dawî” at 12:30 p.m.




In the afternoon, a panel discussion will focus on the portrayal of the Kurdish question in cinema. The guest speaker will be Ali Aydın, director of the films “Küf” and “Kronoloji.” Titled “The Kurdish Question in Cinema,” the discussion will take place at TEV-ÇAND from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. and will be moderated by Berfin Hezil.




Cultural work in Syria and international perspectives




On Wednesday, November 18, Ghasan Halawani’s film “Erased, Ascent of the Invisible” will be screened at Sine Jin between 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. At 12:25 p.m., “Decision,” the fifth and final production in the “Ji Rojava” section, will be screened.




Another panel discussion, titled “Why Is Cultural Work Important in Syria Today?”, will take place at TEV-ÇAND from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. Moderated by Ciwan Tetter, the discussion will bring together Boushra Adi, Khoshman Qado and Muhammad Hajj Hussein to explore the significance of cultural activities and the social conditions in which they take place.




Other screenings scheduled for the day include the Kurdish-language short films “Gazelle” and “Limo Knew Everything,” as well as “Nezouh” by Syrian director Soudade Kaadan.




Filmmaking under dictatorship




On Thursday, November 19, the program will begin at 9:00 a.m. at Sine Jin with a workshop led by director Leena Manimekalai. Drawing on her film “Maadathy – An Unfairy Tale,” she will share her experiences of filmmaking in collaboration with local communities. The workshop will run until 1:00 p.m.




In the afternoon, Syrian director Ossama Mohammed, one of the filmmakers behind “Silvered Water, Syria Self-Portrait,” will discuss filmmaking under dictatorship. The event will take place at TEV-ÇAND from 3:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m.




The evening program will begin at 5:25 p.m. with the Kurdish-language short film “Ishaq,” followed by “Fountain” at 5:45 p.m. and “As We Breathe” at 6:15 p.m.




Festival to conclude with more workshops and an awards ceremony




On Friday, November 20, the focus will once again be on practical filmmaking. Director and writer Liwaa Yazji will lead a workshop at Sine Jin from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., exploring the development of film projects from the initial idea to the screenplay.




From 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., director Soudade Kaadan will offer insights into the screenplay and production process of her film “Aziza” at Hunergeha Welat.




Between 2:00 p.m. and 4:00 p.m., “Ninety” by Lebanese director Maroun Baghdadi will be screened at TEV-ÇAND.




The closing program will begin at 5:00 p.m. at the Mihemed Şêxo Center with a concert by Adnan Karim. The 6th International Rojava Film Festival will conclude at 7:00 p.m. with the presentation of the festival awards.

title: Shengal People’s Council calls for the recognition of the will of Yazidi society
content:
On the 11th anniversary of the liberation of the Yazidi region from the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS), the Shengal People’s Council called for the recognition of the will of Shengal and the Yazidi community.




In a statement on Thursday, the council recalled the resistance against ISIS and the social and political structures established since 2014. It emphasized that the ongoing process of democratic integration into the Iraqi state must be based on recognition of these achievements.




Shengal was liberated on November 13, 2015, following more than a year of fighting against ISIS. The People’s Council particularly honored the efforts of the Kurdish guerrilla forces and Yazidi defense units. It specifically commemorated the fallen commanders Dilşêr Herekol, Egîd Civiyan, Berfîn Nûrhaq, Nûjîn Amed, Çeko Çatak, Saît Hesen, Berxwedan Tolhildan, Dijwar Feqîr and Zerdeşt Şengalî.




“Just as the history of our people has been marked by attacks and fermans, its courageous people have repeatedly written stories of victory through their resistance,” the statement said. The Yazidi community uses the term 

Ferman 

to refer to the historical campaigns of persecution and extermination directed against its people.

title: Koçyiğit: Rojin Kabaiş case extends into state institutions
content:
Gülistan Kılıç Koçyiğit, deputy parliamentary group chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), called for a full investigation into the death of university student Rojin Kabaiş during a press conference at the Turkish parliament. Her remarks followed an attack and threats against the young woman’s uncle in Istanbul. Koçyiğit expressed suspicions that the case involved connections to state institutions and drew parallels with the unresolved disappearance of university student Gülistan Doku.




At the beginning of her press conference, Koçyiğit addressed the explosion at the HABAŞ steel plant in the Aliağa district of Izmir province, which claimed the lives of 19 workers. She criticized the failure to hold those responsible accountable and the lack of adequate state oversight of workplace safety.




“There are no independent inspections, and no one talks to the workers. Instead, they talk to the business owners. Not a single concern raised by employees is heard. Workers are dying because these safety measures would impose costs on employers,” Koçyiğit said.




Another issue addressed at the press conference was the sinking of the Tuğberk İmamoğlu vessel in the Sea of Marmara in September. The families of nine people whose bodies have still not been recovered visited several parliamentary groups the previous day to draw attention to their situation. Koçyiği

title: Students in Rojava: We will not back down until our right to education in Kurdish is recognized
content:
Protests against restrictions on Kurdish-language education continue across Rojava. On Thursday, students, parents and residents demonstrated in Hesekê, Dirbêsiyê and Rimêlan, demanding recognition of Kurdish as an official language of Syria and constitutional guarantees for the right to education in their mother tongue.




In Hesekê, hundreds of people took part in a march that began at the Kevok roundabout and continued to the Şehîd Serhed intersection. Demonstrators carried banners bearing slogans such as “Our language is our identity,” “Our rights must be guaranteed in the constitution,” “Kurdish is our red line” and “Our language is our dignity.”




PYD: Damascus must reverse its decision




At the rally that followed, Ebdulxenî Oso of the Democratic Union Party (PYD) addressed the demonstrators. He recalled the development of Kurdish-language education since the beginning of the Rojava Revolution.




“The identity of peoples is closely linked to their language and culture. In Rojava, the Kurdish language has made significant progress over the past 14 years. Kurdish has been used as the language of instruction in schools, institutes and universities. Today, our language is also used in civilian institutions and public offices,” Oso said.

title: Women in Arzoxlî continue resistance against solar power project
content:
Resistance against the construction of solar power facilities continues in the village of Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar) in the province of Amed (Diyarbakır). Residents have been holding a protest vigil against the Zenkar 1 project for 22 days. During a march from the village square to the planned construction site, Turkish gendarmerie units blocked the path of the protesting women.




The demonstrators chanted slogans such as “Our land and our water are our existence,” “We will prevail through resistance” and “No to the company.” When soldiers prevented them from entering the site, the villagers questioned the legality of their actions: “On what legal grounds are you preventing us from entering our own land?”













“They have bought everything with money”




Emine Eren, who has been participating in the protest vigil, accused the security forces of prioritizing the company’s interests over the rights of the villagers. “There is no humanity left here. People have no heart anymore. They have bought everything with money. There is no justice left to speak of,” she said.




Eren criticized the fact that residents have to protest every day against encroachments on their living environment. “Do we really have to come here every day? Our village has its own resources. title: Two political prisoners released after decades of imprisonment
content:
Political prisoners Aydın Kudat and Zübeyir Idem have been released from Turkish prisons after serving 34 and 30 years, respectively. In both cases, the responsible Administrative and Observation Boards had repeatedly blocked their release despite the completion of their regular prison terms.




Aydın Kudat released after 34 years




Aydın Kudat was released from the T-type prison in Karabük on Wednesday and was welcomed by his family outside the facility. He was arrested in 1992 in the Bismil district of Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) and subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment by the then State Security Court (DGM).




His release was originally scheduled for September 6, 2022. However, the responsible prison board denied his release a total of six times. The stated reason was Kudat’s refusal to sign the so-called declaration of remorse demanded by the prison administration.




The long-term prisoner was finally able to leave prison following a new decision by the board. He was scheduled to return to Amed on Wednesday evening on a flight via Istanbul.




Zübeyir Idem released after two postponements




Zübeyir Idem has also regained his freedom after 30 years in prison. He was released from the prison in Espiye, Giresun province, after the responsible Administrative and Observation Board approved his release.

title: Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik: We must fight the roots of violence against women
content:
Writer Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik spoke to ANF on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, highlighting the direct relationship between the women's struggle and social peace, as well as the connection between male violence and state violence. Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik discussed women's struggle to become active subjects in the process of bringing Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's Call for Peace and Democratic Society of 27 February 2025 into society, as well as the struggle that must be waged against policies of impunity.




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that the Women's Initiative I Need Peace, of which she is a member, was established to bring Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan's Call for Peace and Democratic Society of 27 February 2025 into society and discuss how women could become active subjects in this process. She stated that, as efforts to build social support for peace continue, state violence against women throughout the 40 years of war remains one of the most urgent issues they face.




'Male domination persists under every ruling system'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that women were discussing not only the future but also the past, summarizing the historical transformation of male domination as follows: "Femicide and male violence against women, which continue to exist in human life, have been the most visible manifestations of male domination since its emergence. At the same time, we know that male domination has become a system in its own right, infiltrating and becoming embedded in every dimension of economic, social and political life, regardless of the system in place, and maintaining its existence under every ruling order. This is the reality from which we proceed."




'The same reality lies behind domestic violence and state violence'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik stated that the state is the structure that governs on behalf of the ruling powers in today's world, pointing out that the same state structure stands behind violence, protects male perpetrators through the judiciary and grants reductions in their sentences.




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik recalled that women's bodies and sexuality were targeted through sexual torture and massacres during the 40 years of war, saying, "The same reality lies behind the violence directed at a woman murdered by her husband at home or shot in the street by her ex-husband, and the sexual aggression women encounter at the hands of state police officers, soldiers, village guards or counterterrorism units. And we women are still struggling against this as one of our most fundamental issues."




'Musa Orhan's acquittal is a major cause for outrage'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik strongly condemned the acquittal of Specialist Sergeant Musa Orhan in the case in which he was tried on charges of aggravated sexual assault, emphasizing that a policy of impunity had been implemented despite Ipek Er explicitly identifying the perpetrator in a letter before taking her own life. She recalled that women, journalists, filmmakers and writers who protested against this situation had been punished. Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said, "While state officials are treated with extraordinary privilege, a murderer like Musa Orhan can be acquitted. There is no more striking example that illustrates the situation so clearly. Above all, this is a major cause for outrage."




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik stressed that this situation must occupy a central place in the upcoming 25 November mobilizations against violence against women. She called for all femicides covered up by the state to become a central focus of the struggle, particularly the Gülistan Doku case, which she said had been covered up by a network responsible for murder operating around the governor's office.




'Making people compete over their suffering is a state policy'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that an end to the conflicts would mean that massacres, torture and rape would cease and that this reality would become publicly acknowledged. She also stated that peace would lift the nationalist barriers obstructing class struggle. Pointing out that the 2027 budget had once again been prepared as a "war budget", with no allocation for women, Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik assessed the process as follows: "We need to stand side by side. Making people compete over their suffering is a state policy. When the Call for Peace and Democratic Society was made, those waging the war immediately came forward and asked, 'What will happen to our martyrs and veterans?' Yet this is precisely where both the sharpest edge of oppression and the key to resolving the problems lie. A door has opened, and that door is open to everyone. We must recognize this and organize a strategic approach and sphere of activity that will open that door wider."




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik stated that people could discuss everything in their daily lives, yet the Kurdish question could not be openly discussed by its name. She emphasized that everyone must take responsibility without delay at a time when Alevi, Kurdish and Yazidi identities remain unrecognized and a uniform Sunni-Turkish identity is imposed.




'Turkey does not implement ECtHR rulings'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik said that Turkey's government was pursuing an anti-democratic and fascist practice of power, refusing to implement rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and disregarding court decisions even while exploiting the 12 September Constitution.




She said: "We can see just how anti-democratic Turkey is, with a government that has come to power by exploiting even the 12 September Constitution and refuses to implement court rulings. Turkey is a country that does not implement ECtHR rulings. At a time when imperialist policies around the world are organizing new wars and armament, the People's Leader of the Kurdish Freedom Movement, which has exposed the reality behind all this corruption, is still being held in prison, having been brought there through a conspiracy in the first place. We are confronted with repression and violence that refuse to lift the isolation despite ECtHR rulings."




'

We can develop a powerful struggle against violence'




Mukaddes Erdoğdu Çelik recalled that 25 November emerged from the revolutionary resistance of the Mirabal sisters against state violence in Latin America and concluded: "The meaning of 25 November has expanded considerably in Turkey; state violence and patriarchal violence have merged. This is a very important phenomenon. If we properly understand its significance, we can develop a very powerful struggle against violence from the women's front. However, the women's movement must also make confronting the sources of this violence an essential part of its agenda."
