title: Students demanding education in mother tongue attacked in Hesekê
content:
A demonstration demanding the right to education in the mother tongue was attacked in the northeastern Syrian city of Hesekê. Students had gathered outside the provincial administration building to demand education in their own language. Forces affiliated with the Syrian transitional government intervened against the gathering and fired shots into the air.




According to information obtained by the ANHA news agency, a group believed to be Arab residents from the Xiwêran neighborhood initially attacked the demonstrators with stones. Meanwhile, security forces of the transitional government attempted to disperse the protest and prevent it from continuing, using firearms.




The students condemned the intervention and emphasized the peaceful nature of their demonstration. “What have we done wrong to be prevented from doing this? We took to the streets peacefully and are demanding our right to our own language,” they told ANHA. The protesters also made it clear that the attacks would not deter them from demanding education in their mother tongue.




Since early September, students and their families in Rojava have been protesting against restrictions on Kurdish-language education. The protests were triggered by the Syrian transitional government’s decision to scale back Kurdish-language instruction and limit Kurdish classes to three hours per week. title: Bakırhan visits Figen Yüksekdağ, calls for freedom for political prisoners
content:
Ten years after the wave of arrests targeting the Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP), representatives of several left-wing and democratic parties gathered outside Kandıra Women’s Prison in the western Turkish province of Kocaeli to demand the release of political prisoners. The gathering marked the anniversary of November 4, 2016, when the Turkish government launched a sweeping crackdown on the parliamentary representation of the Kurdish population with the arrests of then-HDP Co-Chairs Figen Yüksekdağ and Selahattin Demirtaş, along with several other members of parliament.




Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), had earlier visited Figen Yüksekdağ, who has been imprisoned for ten years, together with a delegation. Following the visit, party representatives and numerous supporters gathered outside the prison. Under the slogan “Freedom for political prisoners – for peace and democracy,” they demanded the release of those imprisoned.







Bakırhan: The political crackdown of 2016 continues to have repercussions today




Bakırhan described the arrests of November 4, 2016, as a “political coup” whose consequences have long since extended beyond the Kurdish opposition. He said the process had begun with the lifting of parliamentary immunity on May 20, 2016, a move that had also been supported by sections of the opposition at the time.




“On that day, a deep wound was inflicted on Turkey’s political history,” Bakırhan stated. He argued that the violations of rights committed at the time had since expanded to affect nearly all opposition forces. “What was done to the HDP back then is now being directed against all institutions and individuals engaged in opposition activities.”










“This is not just a peace process”




Referring to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process, Bakırhan stated that the continued imprisonment of opposition politicians contradicted the declared objectives of political reconciliation. He stressed that anyone seeking to overcome social polarization must first address past injustices. This includes, in particular, implementing the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) and Turkey’s Constitutional Court, he noted.




“For ten years, we have been standing outside these prisons and making statements. Hasn’t it been enough? In the eleventh year, our friends must once again be able to engage in democratic politics alongside us,” Bakırhan said. He stressed that Figen Yüksekdağ should be able to advocate her political position on peace outside prison. Selahattin Demirtaş, too, should be reunited with his people and his political colleagues, he said.




“This is not just a peace process. It is also a process of democratization,” the DEM Party Co-Chair emphasized. He remarked that prisons must be emptied for Turkey to achieve the rule of law, justice and democracy. Alongside Yüksekdağ and Demirtaş, he named several imprisoned politicians and activists, including Can Atalay, Osman Kavala, Bekir Kaya and Leyla Güven. He stressed that their place was not in prison but in society.




Left-wing parties demand an end to political prosecutions




Representatives of socialist parties also linked their demands for the release of political prisoners to fundamental democratic rights. Sezin Uçar, Deputy Co-Chair of the Socialist Party of the Oppressed (ESP), recalled the decade-long resistance against political persecution.




“Without freedom of expression, protest and organization, we can neither achieve peace nor build democracy,” she stated. Uçar said the ESP was demanding the release of all political prisoners, the repeal of Turkey’s Anti-Terror Law and the removal of all restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly and organization. She specifically highlighted those imprisoned in connection with the Kobanê and Gezi trials.













Levent Tüzel, Deputy Chair of the Labour Party (EMEP), described the Kobanê trial as a politically motivated prosecution. He pointed out that the HDP had been justified in calling for solidarity with the resistance against the siege of Kobanê in 2014. According to Tüzel, however, the protests at the time had been manipulated by paramilitary forces, with responsibility for the violence subsequently attributed to the HDP leadership. Tüzel criticized the lengthy prison sentences imposed as a result. He emphasized that the demand of peoples to live together in equality and freedom was at the heart of the current peace process.













Öztürk demands concrete steps from the government




Hakan Öztürk, Chair of the Labour Movement Party (EHP), called on the Turkish government to follow up its political statements and legislative measures with concrete action. Otherwise, he warned, the peace process risked losing credibility.




“If the reports that have been prepared and the promises that have been made were not merely empty words, they must now be put into practice. Otherwise, seriousness and trust will be lost,” Öztürk said.




Öztürk stated that the Kurdish movement and Abdullah Öcalan had made their contribution to changing the political climate. He said that this development must now also be reflected in Öcalan’s prison conditions and ability to work. In particular, Öztürk called for the establishment of the previously announced body for peace and political participation, which is intended to coordinate the further implementation of the process.




The EHP Chair also demanded the release of the politicians imprisoned in Kandıra, arguing that they had been deprived of their freedom through politically motivated court rulings and should be released immediately.

title: Kurdish writer Gülazer Akın released after 30 years in prison
content:
Kurdish political prisoner and writer Gülazer Akın has been released from Bünyan Women’s Prison in Turkey’s Kayseri province after 30 years of imprisonment. She was welcomed outside the prison by family members, representatives of the prisoners’ solidarity association TUHAYDER and numerous supporters. Akın, who had been imprisoned since November 1996, endured numerous health problems during her decades behind bars, completed a university degree and wrote several literary works.




Upon her release, Akın said she had not believed until the very end that she would actually be able to leave prison. The release of a fellow prisoner had previously been postponed by a decision of the Prison Administration and Observation Board. She therefore feared that her own release might also be blocked.




“As long as even one of our friends remains in prison, I will not feel that I have truly been released,” Akın said. She also welcomed the peace process that had begun: “We have matured and returned. A new process has begun. I said this before the board as well. A new process has begun, and I support it. There is probably nothing more beautiful than freedom.”




Following her remarks, Akın released a white dove as a symbol of peace.




TUHAY-DER calls for the release of political prisoners




During the welcome gathering, the prisoners’ solidarity association TUHAY-DER criticized the continued imprisonment of seriously ill prisoners and the repeated postponement of scheduled releases. Representatives of the association stated that genuine freedom could only be achieved when all political prisoners and Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan were released.




The decisions of Prison Administration and Observation Boards have faced criticism from human rights and prisoners’ rights organizations for years. These organizations accuse the boards of delaying the release of long-term prisoners for political reasons, despite their having met the necessary requirements for release.




Three decades behind prison walls




Gülazer Akın was born in 1975 in Ahlat, in the province of Bitlis. She joined the Kurdish freedom movement in 1993. On November 3, 1996, she was arrested in Istanbul and placed in pretrial detention. A Turkish State Security Court later sentenced her to life imprisonment on charges of separatism.




During her imprisonment, Akın was held in various prisons across Turkey. Despite health problems, she continued her education and graduated with a degree in public administration from Anadolu University.




At the same time, she devoted herself extensively to literature. Her experiences of imprisonment, social exclusion and women’s lives became central themes in her writing.




Writing against oblivion




Akın’s first novel, 

Tencerenin Dibi

 (

The Bottom of the Cooking Pot

), was published in 2013. The book was introduced by Turkish writer Adil Okay, who drew attention to the extraordinary circumstances under which she produced her literary work in an accompanying text.




Okay quoted from a letter Akın had written after 18 years of imprisonment. In it, she described how an entire generation had grown up behind prison walls while life continued outside:




“We were still almost children when we entered prison. Many of us grew up and matured while staring at walls. As the walls deteriorated, we grew more mature.”




Akın offered a particularly poignant account of her encounters with family members whose growth she could witness only during prison visits:




“When we entered prison, our siblings, nieces and nephews were still babies. Today, they are adults. We could only watch all of this through the small window of the prison. With every visit, we were amazed all over again and asked: When did you grow so big?”




According to Akın, this experience created an almost unbearable sense of injustice. Adil Okay praised her novel as a work written under conditions in which even colored pencils had reportedly been prohibited. Despite these restrictions, the writer developed her own literary voice to bring attention to experiences that were barely acknowledged beyond the prison walls.




Confronting patriarchal social structures




With her 2017 book 

Cinsiyetçiliğin Yaratımı

 (

The Creation of Sexism

), Akın also turned her attention to theoretical questions concerning women’s liberation. In the book, she examines sexism as a system of social domination and explores the significance of women’s self-determination in transforming social structures.




“We know that sexism is a male construct,” Akın writes. She emphasizes that women have both the right and the need to understand themselves, develop their abilities and independently determine their role in society.




She views women’s liberation not merely as individual emancipation but as a foundation for building a society based on solidarity and coexistence.

title: Ecocide continues in Şırnak: Hundreds of oak trees cut down
content:
Environmental destruction continues in the Kurdish province of Şırnak. Footage recorded by local residents yesterday in the Besta region shows hundreds of oak trees cut down across a vast area, leaving large sections of the forest stripped of trees.




While activities carried out under the guise of mining exploration on Mount Cudi and oil exploration on Mount Gabar for nearly a decade have already caused significant environmental damage, tree felling continues in the Besta region under the pretext of commercial activity.




According to reports, oak trees, some of them up to a century old, have been cut down by village guards under military supervision. Footage recorded in the Kaniya Kolanan and Dergê Gêzna areas showed numerous trees being cut down at their bases with chainsaws. The logging site is reportedly accessible only through a military checkpoint, and around ten people were said to be operating in the area with vans and chainsaws.




DEM Party Şırnak MP Mehmet Zeki İrmez shared the footage on his social media account, condemning the tree felling and tagging the Şırnak Governor’s Office and the Provincial Directorate of Agriculture.

content:

Every Wednesday, activists stage a protest in front of the United Nations building to demand the release of Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan. The action is carried out as part of the 'Dem dema azadiye' [Time for Freedom] campaign and is directed against the isolation of the Kurdish leader on the Turkish prison island of Imrali, the Turkish occupation attacks on Kurdistan, the massacres committed in Kurdish territories and the silence of the UN. Demonstratos call on international institutions to fulfill their responsibilities to secure Öcalan’s physical freedom.




This week's demonstration, which is held at a tent set up in Nations Square where the UN Office is located, began with a moment of silence in memory of those who lost their lives in the Kurdish freedom struggle.




During this week’s demonstration, participants from Kurdistan once again called on international institutions to fulfill their responsibilities in securing the physical freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan, who has been held in Imralı Island Prison since 1999.

title: Rojhilat Alliance: Member parties in favor of continuing dialogue
content:
The Rojhilat Kurdistan Union Group issued a written statement regarding its meeting with representatives of four member parties of the Alliance of Political Forces of Eastern Kurdistan.




The statement said: “In order to activate the Alliance of Political Forces of Eastern Kurdistan, which was established more than eight months ago, and to identify the obstacles preventing it from functioning effectively, the Rojhilat Kurdistan Union Group invited the Alliance’s six parties to a consultative meeting.




The Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK), the Organization of Struggle of Iranian Kurdistan (Sazmana Xebat a Kurdistana Îranê), the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (KDP-I), and the Association of Kurdistan Toilers attended the meeting.

title: German ambassador visits Amed Metropolitan Municipality
content:
The German Ambassador to Turkey, Sibylle Katharina Sorg, visited Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) Metropolitan Municipality. Accompanied by Embassy Secretary Nicole Gonsior, she was received by Serra Bucak and Emin Ay, the co-mayors of the DEM Party-run metropolitan municipality.

title: Ağın: A united struggle is needed to democratise Turkey - Part One
content:
Writer and politician Ömer Ağın stated that the main obstacle to the Peace and Democratic Society Process was the state's failure to take concrete steps towards a democratic solution.




Ağın emphasised that democratic mass organisations, trade unions and professional associations must join the struggle for the process to advance, highlighting the importance of uniting around current democratic demands.




Ömer Ağın recalled the historical roots of the Kurdish question and the state's security-oriented approach, stating that a solution required time and mutual determination. Ağın said, "This process involves longstanding difficulties and deep-rooted problems. The Kurdish question is undoubtedly one of Turkey's most important and complex issues."




Ağın continued: "The issue has historical roots, and there are grievances that have accumulated on both sides from the founding of the Republic to the present day. The Kurdish people have no trust in the state, governments or the regime. Throughout the Republican period, almost every government has treated the Kurdish question as a security issue, a terrorism issue, and has attempted to suppress it through repression. This approach continues today. These attitudes remain deeply embedded throughout the system. Because this is a multidimensional issue, it is not easy to make progress or resolve the problem overnight. Everyone acknowledges this.




The Kurdish movement says so, and so do reasonable people. The Kurdish movement's own assessments also indicate that the issue can only be resolved through a process. It has been stated that this is merely the first step. Nobody expects everything to be resolved overnight. But what matters here is the approach being taken. Are there genuinely sincere intentions to resolve this issue? How do the parties view it? At what stage is society? What is society's ideological, political and organisational position? When we examine these questions, it is difficult to offer a particularly encouraging or reassuring assessment."




Ağın stated that he considered the Kurdish movement's approach to a solution sincere, emphasising its demands for dialogue and negotiations, the protection of democratic rights and an end to repression. 




Ağın said: "The Kurdish movement, the Kurds and the demands and aspirations of the Kurdish people are sincere. They genuinely want this issue to be resolved and to obtain their democratic rights. They want the repression and violence directed against them to end and the violations of their rights and values to be brought to an end. They are making efforts towards this goal, and their demands are sincere. The Kurdish movement has now recognised, in terms of its social values, organisational structure, ideological and political position and paradigm of struggle, that this issue can be resolved through dialogue and negotiations. It has understood that violence, repression and mutual conflict benefit no one. It believes that the Kurdish question can only be resolved through democratic and peaceful methods, within a framework of mutual rights and the rule of law.




There may be certain shortcomings on the Kurdish side and within Kurdish society in understanding, embracing and advancing the process. An adequate organisational structure may not yet have been established. Nevertheless, they are sincere in their ideas, paradigms and demands."




‘The process has become a whirlpool’




Ağın stated that the struggle for political power among Turkey's political forces had overshadowed the democratisation process, while parties' political calculations were slowing efforts to resolve the Kurdish question and secure common democratic gains for the peoples.




Ağın said: "This process has become a whirlpool. In Kurdish, a whirlpool is called 'gerînet'. It describes swirling water that draws in and engulfs everything around it. From a social perspective, the process appears to have entered such a whirlpool. Many people share this view.




I believe the Kurdish movement is aware of this. Because it knows that overcoming this situation will not be easy, it attaches importance to social values and shows patience in seeking to remove the obstacles to Turkey's democratisation. Today, there is the Republican People's Party (CHP), as well as the newly established party. The struggle and conflict for political power between these groups, particularly between the new party and the Justice and Development Party (AKP), have also turned into a whirlpool. Turkey's democratisation seems to have become almost entirely a struggle for power among these forces. For this reason, there is little evidence of a sincere approach or concrete steps towards democratisation. Pragmatic approaches and tactical calculations have come to the forefront.




Efforts that could contribute to the democratisation of Turkey, Kurdistan and the Middle East, and to common democratic gains for Kurds, Turks, Arabs, Circassians and all peoples, are progressing slowly. This is one of the main reasons for the current deadlock."




‘The state must take concrete steps’




Ömer Ağın pointed out that the state was dragging its feet over the process and had yet to take concrete steps. He stressed that the calls being made must be translated into practice.




Ağın said: "The government and the state, which have been slowing down this process, have not yet taken any serious steps. Looking at the current balance of power, there is little indication of a sincere willingness to take significant steps in the near future. Since the beginning of the process, Devlet Bahçeli has made various appeals in his speeches, such as 'Let them come and talk.' But how sincere are these appeals? How much influence do they have on the government? What is the state's overall position on this issue? These questions need to be examined seriously.




It is difficult to speak of any significant progress in practice because no concrete steps have been taken. A framework law has been introduced, and yes, this is something that should be regarded as important. But from this point onwards, the government's position, the statements of its spokespersons and the remarks of officials must be subjected to a test of sincerity. I do not believe that a particularly sincere approach has been demonstrated."




‘Democratisation cannot be achieved through the Kurdish people's struggle alone’




Ömer Ağın stated that a democratic solution to the Kurdish question would only be possible if different sections of society united around common demands.




Ağın continued: "A struggle limited to the Kurds cannot achieve results. It seems very difficult to overcome the obstacles facing this process through slogans based solely on their demands. Society as a whole, Turks, people living in western Turkey, democratic mass organisations, trade unions and professional associations must actively support this process. The democratisation of Turkish society and the successful, lasting continuation of the process cannot be achieved through the Kurdish people's struggle alone.




Those involved in politics in western Turkey, political parties and democratic mass organisations have not yet sufficiently recognised that resolving the Kurdish question through democratic methods would benefit Kurds, Turks and the Middle East, or that this is one of the fundamental issues in Turkey's democratisation. Nor have they reached the point of actively struggling for it. It also seems unlikely that they will mobilise solely around the Kurdish people's slogans or demands for certain forms of recognition of Abdullah Öcalan's status.




The demands of society in western Turkey and other sections suffering under the regime must also be brought together around the Kurdish question in a broader sense. Strategies and policies must be developed to achieve this. The demands for Mr. Öcalan's freedom, the recognition of the Kurdish people's demands, transparent negotiations and the free participation of democratic forces in the negotiation process are legitimate and entirely justified. Nevertheless, a large proportion of the Turkish population in western Turkey has not yet been convinced that this is the path towards democracy. This presents a problem. There is a need to broaden these demands and put forward more concrete proposals.




One of the most important issues is the situation in prisons. Kurds face serious difficulties. Many people have spent 30 years in prison and remain incarcerated despite having completed their sentences. People from the former ranks of the CHP, individuals associated with the newly established party, and the Mayor of Istanbul are also in prison. There are also people affiliated with religious orders who are imprisoned. In other words, prisons hold people from many different sections of society. This is a serious problem."

title: Students in Kobanê reject incorporation of their university
content:
Students and staff at the University of Kobanê have rejected plans to incorporate their institution into the University of Aleppo. In a statement marking World Kobanê Day on November 1, they called for the university’s institutional autonomy to be preserved and for no decisions about its future to be made without the participation of its students and staff. They explicitly stated that they were not opposed to cooperation with other Syrian universities.




The statement was read out by student Gulistan Elî in front of the university building in Kobanê, in the presence of faculty members and students. It came in response to a recent decision by the Syrian Ministry of Higher Education to integrate the University of Kobanê into the state higher education system.




Opposition despite agreement with Damascus




Just on Saturday, the university administration announced the outcome of further negotiations with the Syrian government. According to the agreement, the University of Kobanê is to be incorporated into the University of Aleppo as a group of faculties while retaining its own administrative structures. Students already enrolled will be allowed to complete their studies under the existing system. Recognition of their degrees has also been guaranteed.

title: Geothermal project in Varto: Court examines potential environmental damage
content:
A court-ordered site inspection has taken place as part of a legal dispute over a planned geothermal project on the border between the Kurdish provinces of Bingöl and Muş. A panel of experts appointed by the Bingöl Administrative Court examined the proposed drilling sites in the villages of Licik, Çermî, and Şorik in the Karlıova district. Local residents fear that the project will severely threaten their livelihoods and are demanding its cancellation.




The project, undertaken by the US-based company IGNIS H2 Energy, covers an area between Karlıova and Varto. Affected residents filed a lawsuit against the project in April. In July, the court ordered an expert assessment and an on-site inspection.




Concerns over water sources and agriculture




Numerous local residents participated in the inspection on Monday. The expert panel was accompanied by DEM Party MPs Ibrahim Akın and Sümeyye Boz, lawyers from the Diyarbakır Bar Association, and representatives of various environmental organizations from Kurdistan and Turkey.













Akın, who also serves as co-spokesperson for the DEM Party’s Ecology Commission, highlighted the local population’s ongoing resistance. He stated that the inspections would extend from Bingöl to the Varto region.

author: Unknown
title: 29 women killed in Southern Kurdistan in ten months
content:
In the first ten months of 2026, at least 29 women were victims of femicide in Southern Kurdistan. Another 29 women died under suspicious circumstances, according to a recent analysis by the Roj News agency. Three women were killed in October alone.




On October 15, a 20-year-old woman was killed by her brother, who was eight years older than her, in the Domîz subdistrict of Sêmêlê district near Duhok. Five days later, on October 20, 30-year-old Kîjan Burhan was murdered by her father, who shot her three times, in Sulaymaniyah.




The third case was reported on October 29 in the village of Şêx Turab near Hewlêr (Erbil), where the body of a murdered woman was discovered. Four suspects were arrested, and police in Hewlêr launched an investigation.




Women’s organizations have long criticized domestic violence as one of the most serious social problems in Southern Kurdistan. They are calling for effective prevention and intervention measures aimed at preventing violence, protecting victims, and bringing about lasting changes in violent patterns of behavior.

title: ISIG: At least 678 migrants died on their workplace in six years
content:
Data compiled from reports by ISIG (Health and Safety Labour Observatory) show that migrant and refugee workers accounted for 4.8 percent of the 14,110 workers killed in workplace accidents between 2020 and the first nine months of 2026. Four workers were killed and another was injured when a tornado struck Antalya during the night of 26 October. Antalya Governor Hulusi Şahin said that the tornado had torn apart two containers housing workers employed at a residential construction site.




A judicial investigation was launched following the deaths of the four workers. Four people, including the construction contractor and site manager, were detained as part of the investigation.




Three of the workers were refugees




The workers who lost their lives were identified as Aycan Kılınç, Muhammed El Omar, Isa Elnevvah and Muhammed El Zeyn. The fact that three of the workers were Syrian brought renewed attention to the deaths of migrant and refugee workers in workplace accidents in Turkey in recent years.




Annual reports by ISIG provide information on deaths among migrant and refugee workers. According to ISIG reports, at least 678 migrant and refugee workers were killed in workplace accidents between 2020 and September 2026. The Observatory's annual reports show that a total of 12,374 workers were killed in workplace accidents between 2020 and 2025.

content:

‘Different sections of society perceive the process differently’

Fatma Bostan Ünsal said: "We can see that different sections of society in Turkey perceive this process very differently, from its name to its content. title: Peace Mothers arrive in Ankara
content:
Members of the Peace Mothers’ Assembly, who set out from 24 cities demanding that Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom be secured, that prisoners be released, and that concrete steps be taken as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, have arrived in Ankara.




The mothers gathered at the headquarters of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) in Balgat.




The Peace Mothers will make a statement at Parliament Park to publicize their demands, then hold a tent vigil at Kurtuluş Park.




Buses from Istanbul, Izmir, Van and Amed




The Istanbul Peace Mothers’ Assembly traveled to Ankara by bus last night. 







Members of the Izmir Peace Mothers’ Assembly held a press conference last night at the Izmir provincial headquarters of the Democratic Regions Party (DBP), where they had gathered before setting off for Ankara. During the statement, slogans were repeatedly chanted, including “There can be no life without the Leader,” “Long live Leader Apo,” and “Woman, life, freedom.”




Speaking on behalf of the group, Peace Mother Behiye Yalçın recalled that the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which began with Öcalan’s 27 February call, had been underway for two years.




Behiye Yalçın said: “There are certain deadlocks. Peace Mothers from Turkey and Kurdistan have been turning toward Ankara since early this morning. We will set off for Ankara shortly.

title: Independent Engineers and Architects: It is not natural disasters but greed and negligence that kill
content:
Heavy rainfall affecting many cities, particularly Istanbul, has once again exposed the inadequacy of urban infrastructure and the devastating consequences of profit-driven urban development policies. Flooding turned underpasses and tunnels into lakes, bringing transport and daily life almost to a standstill. Five people lost their lives in the floods. According to the governor's office, authorities recorded 1,277 flooding incidents, 15 landslides, 47 reports of people stranded, 13 fallen trees, and reports involving 76 vehicles, 808 homes and 280 workplaces.




The Istanbul Platform of Independent Engineers, Architects and Urban Planners spoke to ANF following the devastation, which has reached deadly proportions. The platform stressed that the real cause of the disaster was not the weather but a profit-driven and negligent mentality that disregards both nature and human life.




‘Disadvantaged sections of society are once again paying the price’




The platform drew attention to the political and social realities behind the destruction, which the government and business interests have sought to dismiss as a 'natural disaster'. It stressed that, as always, low-income and disadvantaged sections of society were bearing the heaviest burden. content:
Peace Mothers from 24 cities gathered in Ankara to demand the physical freedom of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan and concrete steps within the framework of the peace and democratic society process. Carrying a banner reading “Take steps for peace, Parliament must act,” the mothers chanted slogans including “A thousand greetings to Imralı,” “Long live the resistance in the prisons,” and “Women do not want war, they want peace.”




Speaking on behalf of the group, Peace Mother Meryem Korkmaz stated that Öcalan’s legal status had still not been recognized. “The architect of peace is still on Imralı. We demand that the promises made be fulfilled and that steps be taken toward peace. We have always stood for peace. We do not accept any interruption of this process. Steps must be taken without delay. Our leader’s status must be secured, and the prisoners must be released. Only then can peace be achieved,” she said.




Peace Mother Mürvet Demir stated: “We will not stop until peace is achieved. There will be no peace until our leader’s status is secured and those in prison and in the mountains return. There will be no peace until our leader reunites with his people. That is why we are here.”

title: Aygül Yağış: Save our young people from drugs
content:
Alongside special warfare policies, drug use, betting, gambling, gang activity and incidents of individual violence are among the major social problems in Kurdistan. Field studies conducted by civil society organisations and bar associations indicate that addiction is becoming increasingly widespread, particularly among young people, while families continue to call for solutions. According to available data, the age at which children begin using drugs has fallen to as low as nine, while a significant proportion of users are first introduced to drugs through their friends.




Reports published in the media indicate that 71.2 percent of drug users were first introduced to drugs between the ages of 15 and 24, while 74.4 percent first obtained drugs from friends or people in their immediate social circles. The Turkish Green Crescent's 2025 Gambling Report also highlighted that the age at which people begin gambling has fallen to 15.




According to data from the Diyarbakır (Amed) Bar Association, lawyers were appointed to represent 2,173 people prosecuted for drug production and trafficking between 1 January and 9 September 2023. Lawyers were also appointed to represent 291 people accused of drug use or purchasing, accepting or possessing drugs for personal use.

content:
Members of the Peace Mothers’ Council from 24 cities are continuing their protest in Ankara, where they gathered earlier today. Following a press statement at Parliament Park, the mothers moved to Kurtuluş Park, where they began their vigil.

title: ‘No independent investigations conducted into murders of journalist in the Kurdistan Region’
content:
The Metro Center for Journalists’ Rights and Advocacy issued a statement on the occasion of November 2, the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, designated by the United Nations (UN) in 2013.




The statement read: “In the Kurdistan Region, no independent investigations into the murders of journalists have been conducted because the judiciary is under the influence of the ruling political parties. Cases that have sparked widespread public outrage, such as the murders of Soran Mame Heme, Serdeşt Osman, Kawa Germiyani, Vedat Hüseyin, and Abdülstar Tahir Şerif, remain unsolved. Neither those who carried out the murders nor those who ordered them have been identified or brought to justice.”




Calling for the investigations into these cases to be reopened, the Metro Center drew attention to statements issued by UNESCO, stating: “Impunity for crimes leads to an increase in murders and violence and undermines the legal and justice systems. UNESCO warns that such impunity allows serious human rights violations and corruption to be concealed, causing harm to society as a whole. For this reason, the government, civil society organizations, and media outlets are being urged to uphold the rule of law and support international initiatives aimed at putting an end to such practices.”

content:

Accompanied by members of the Central Executive Board (MYK) and members of parliament, co-chairs of the DEM Party visited the Peace Mothers.













Speaking here, Tülay Hatimoğulları said, “You are the ones who deserve peace the most and have struggled the hardest for it.”




Hatimoğulları noted that the Peace Mothers have consistently fought for peace in public spaces and squares to put an end to suffering. She said, “At the current stage of the peace and democratic society process, you have taken to the roads and come to Ankara to help accelerate the process and enable us to achieve peace sooner.”













The DEM Party co-chair added, “Our visit today is, of course, intended to express both our solidarity with the Peace Mothers, with whom we have walked this path together, and our commitment to our shared struggle. We will most certainly bring peace to this country and these lands. Peace will be established in this land as pure as your white headscarves, with the same dignity and integrity they represent. This is our promise.”

title: Meral Beştaş: The process is facing a serious deadlock
content:

Meral Beştaş pointed out that Kurdish demands for democratic rights and freedoms had been pushed into the background of political discussions. ‘Political will must be translated into concrete steps’

content:

They are demanding the physical freedom of Abdullah Öcalan, the release of political prisoners, and concrete steps toward implementing the peace and democratic society process. Before their departure, the women gathered at two meeting points in Van and Amed (Diyarbakır).




In Van, Peace Mothers from Tatvan and Hakkari joined local participants at Musa Anter Park. Chanting slogans such as “Long live the resistance in the prisons” and “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî – Freedom for the leader,” they set off for Ankara.




In Amed, Peace Mothers from Siirt and Batman, together with activists from local women’s groups, gathered at the Human Rights Monument in Koşuyolu Park. Chanting “Long live the resistance of the mothers” and “Long live the resistance in the prisons,” they reaffirmed their demands.




Speaking on behalf of the assembled women, Afife Kartal stated that the Peace Mothers were no longer willing to accept the continuation of the political process without concrete steps from the Turkish government.

title: People of Kobanê celebrate World Kobanê Day
content:
World Kobanê Day was marked with a public celebration in Kobanê on November 1. Under the slogan “In memory of the heroic martyrs – Long live World Kobanê Day,” large numbers of people gathered to commemorate the resistance against the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS) in 2014 and those who lost their lives. The event focused on the historical significance of the resistance, the leading role of women, and the defense of the achievements of the revolution in Rojava.




The celebration began with a minute of silence in memory of the martyrs. Ferhan Hec Îsa then addressed the gathering on behalf of the people of Kobanê. He paid tribute to those who had defended the city against ISIS attacks and made its liberation possible.




“November 1, World Kobanê Day, is not merely a day of remembrance on the calendar. This date represents the epic resistance through which the people of Kobanê rose up against the attacks of dark forces in 2014 and emerged victorious. Today, Kobanê is known worldwide as a city that has entered the history of resistance and dignity through its struggle against ISIS,” Hec Îsa said.




He called for the achievements won through the struggle to be preserved: “Kobanê is a city that belongs to all of us. We must defend the achievements of the resistance of Kobanê.”

title: Women’s conference in Ankara criticizes stagnation in the peace process
content:
The stalled peace process in Turkey and the responsibility of politicians and society to achieve a democratic solution to the Kurdish question dominated the second day of the women’s conference in Ankara. Discussions focused on the lack of concrete political steps, the unequal conditions surrounding negotiations with Abdullah Öcalan, and how women from different social and political backgrounds could work together to achieve lasting peace. Participants made it clear that while they regarded an end to the armed conflict as a crucial step forward, they did not consider it sufficient in itself to guarantee peace in society.




The conference, titled “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side,” was initiated by 80 women and opened on Saturday with more than 500 participants. On the second day, female politicians, academics, and activists gathered at the Chamber of Civil Engineers to discuss political responsibility for peace, the role of parliament, and opportunities for grassroots organizing.




Buldan warns of deadlock in the peace process




Pervin Buldan, a DEM Party MP and member of the Imralı delegation, recalled the failed peace negotiations between 2013 and 2015 and the subsequent ten years of armed conflict. title: TEV-DEM calls for guarantees for Kurdish rights and protection of achievements
content:
On the occasion of World Kobanê Day on November 1, the Movement for a Democratic Society (TEV-DEM) and its Women’s Council issued separate statements commemorating the historic resistance against the so-called Islamic State (ISIS).




While TEV-DEM emphasized Kobanê’s significance in the struggle for democracy and human dignity and warned against one-sided integration in Syria, the Women’s Council focused on the role of women in defending the city and safeguarding their political and social achievements.




‘Integration does not mean assimilation’

The movement pointed out that the defense of the city had become a global symbol of freedom, social diversity, and the protection of human dignity. “The international solidarity shown by democratic movements, intellectuals, and numerous prominent figures demonstrated that the struggle for humanity transcended both national and religious boundaries,” it underlined.




Regarding the political restructuring of Syria, the movement warned against attempts to exclude Kurds from the process of building the new state or disregard their achievements. title: Humanitarian conditions deteriorate in Washokani and Al-Talae camps
content:
The humanitarian conditions of displaced families living in the Washokani and Al-Talae camps in Syria’s Hesekê Governorate have further deteriorated following recent rainfall and flooding. The Serêkaniyê Displaced Persons Committee has called for urgent shelter assistance ahead of winter season and for the process of returning families to their hometowns to be expedited.




Speaking to Shafaq News, committee spokesperson Mahmud Cemîl said that the tents in both camps had deteriorated and could no longer provide adequate protection against rain, cold weather and extreme heat. Cemîl said the committee had been requesting support and new tents from humanitarian organisations for seven years, but these requests had not been adequately addressed.




Returns should accelerate




Cemîl said that displaced families were facing administrative delays and various obstacles in returning to their hometowns. He called on the Syrian government to expand organised return convoys and increase the number of families able to return.




Cemîl also urged the Syrian presidential delegation overseeing the return process, international organisations and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to support efforts to accelerate returns before winter conditions make life in the camps even more difficult.

title: 7,000-year-old architectural model discovered in Soran
content:
The General Directorate of Antiquities and Cultural Heritage of the Kurdistan Region has announced a significant archaeological discovery at Banahîlk Hill in the Soran district, northeast of Erbil.




In a statement, the directorate said that a rare model of an ancient building's roofing system, dating back more than 7,000 years and belonging to the Halaf culture, had been discovered. Describing the find as a first in archaeological history, the statement noted that it demonstrates the advanced engineering and architectural skills of communities during that period.




The discovery was announced to the public at a press conference held on 28 October at the Scientific Research Centre of Soran University. The archaeological project was carried out in cooperation with the Soran Directorate of Antiquities and Culture, the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Salahaddin University.




The Halaf culture, dating approximately from 6100 to 5100 BC, was influential mainly across the lands of Southern Kurdistan (Başûr), Western Kurdistan (Rojava) and Northern Kurdistan (Bakurê Kurdistan). Known for its distinctive pottery decorated with geometric patterns and animal motifs, this culture provides important archaeological evidence of the prehistoric history of Mesopotamia and the Near East.

title: DEM Party’s message on 1 November, World Kobanê Day
content:
The DEM Party’s Central Executive Board (MYK) issued a written statement to mark 1 November, World Kobanê Day. The statement said: "On 15 September 2014, ISIS, which is hostile to different faiths, identities, cultures and the will of peoples to live together, launched a major attack on Kobanê. In response to the ISIS gangs’ assault on Kobanê, the peoples of the world—particularly the Kurdish people—and internationalist resistance fighters who travelled to Kobanê from all corners of the globe waged an epic resistance against ISIS.




Faced with this historic resistance, which lasted 134 days, the ISIS gangs and the forces behind them suffered a major defeat. The victory won in Kobanê, embraced by peoples across the world and marking a turning point in the beginning of a new history in the Middle East, carries even greater international significance today."




The statement added: "Developed under the leadership of the women’s struggle, the Kobanê resistance laid the groundwork for the Kurdish people to secure their identity-related, cultural and historical rights. It also enabled the development of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which today represents a hope for an equal and free life.

title: Kongra Star calls to continue to protect the city on World Kobanê Day
content:
Kongra Star issued a statement to mark 1 November, World Kobanê Day. The statement commemorated the historic sacrifices made in the fight against ISIS mercenaries in 2014, while highlighting the current and future challenges Kobanê is facing.




The statement paid tribute to the martyrs of the resistance, particularly Arin Mirkan. It stressed that the determination demonstrated by the resistance was no longer confined to the city's geographical boundaries, but had become deeply rooted in humanity's collective memory and conscience as a struggle for freedom and human dignity, placing an ongoing responsibility on everyone to preserve these values.




The statement noted that 1 November represents an "epic of resilience" by a people who refused to bow to darkness. It said that, through their unwavering determination and international solidarity from across the world, the resistance fighters managed to break the siege of the city and repel ISIS attacks, turning Kobanê into an international symbol of ISIS's defeat and a renewed source of hope for peoples worldwide.




Kongra Star underlined that what happened in Kobanê went beyond the military defence of a city, representing instead a defence of a model of coexistence, equality and solidarity that transcends political, linguistic and ideological boundaries. title: Mining destroys Chaldean village's nature and heritage
content:

The surroundings of the village, which were covered in greenery in 2015 and earlier, are now almost entirely devoid of vegetation. The mining sites are reportedly located on the village's former settlement area, and almost no trees remain in the region. Ecological destruction in Botan accelerated with the intensification of the war in 2015.




For years, Botan's natural environment, much of which has been declared off-limits, has been destroyed under military supervision and through the activities of village guards. The ecological destruction that began with forest fires has continued through tree felling, mining and oil exploration.




The mountain's silhouette has changed

title: Özgür Sevgi Göral: France’s dilemmas also exist in Turkey - Part One
content:
Academic Özgür Sevgi Göral said that a strong voice had emerged against inequality in Paris, adding, "Reducing the revolt of the suburbs, which demands profound transformation, to presidential elections would dilute the movement's anger and enthusiasm." Göral said that all the dilemmas facing France were also present in Turkey.




The streets of Paris have witnessed some of the most intense social mobilisation of recent times. Protests that began in September, led by high school students, grew into a mass movement day by day.




ANF spoke to Özgür Sevgi Göral, who is currently in Paris and has participated in the demonstrations, about the historical foundations of the protests and their potential.




Academic Özgür Sevgi Göral emphasised that the protests were rooted in a historical accumulation of struggles, saying, "This history includes the inequalities created by racialised capitalism and the many different forms of violence it has spread throughout everyday life."  Göral stressed the importance of the struggle, saying, "The struggle truly is endless, and despite all the difficult conditions, millions of people around the world refuse to abandon the streets."

title: İpek Er’s mother: My daughter was killed a second time
content:
“My daughter was killed a second time today.” With these words, Hikmet Kılınç, the mother of Kurdish woman İpek Er, who died in 2020, protested the recent acquittal of former gendarmerie officer Musa Orhan at a women’s conference in Ankara. Six years after her daughter’s death, she has leveled serious accusations against state officials and announced her determination to continue her fight for justice all the way to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).




The protest follows a ruling issued on October 22 by a criminal court in Batman. Musa Orhan, who was sentenced to ten years in prison in 2021 for a serious sexual assault against İpek Er, was acquitted of the charge of incitement to suicide in a separate trial. According to Kılınç, the decision represents another setback in her years-long struggle to secure legal accountability for her daughter’s death.




Addressing more than 500 participants at the “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, Kılınç recounted her experiences since her daughter’s death. She accused state authorities of exploiting her hopes for justice and attempting to exert political pressure on her. “For six years, they told me: If you stay away from the Kurdish parties, we will ensure justice for your daughter. title: Shengal People’s Council call for the recognition of the city’s special status
content:
The Shengal People’s Council issued a statement regarding the democratic integration process underway in the city. The statement, which also marked World Kobanê Day on November 1, recalled that both Shengal and Kobanê were besieged by ISIS militants in 2014 and that a new phase of struggle had begun in both Rojava and Shengal after 12 years of resistance.




The Council welcomed the democratic integration process, describing it as the first time in more than a thousand years that a state had recognized the will of the Yazidi community and announced an agreement reached with the freely chosen representatives of the Yazidi people.




The Council further stated that democratic integration in Shengal encompassed not only the YBŞ-YJŞ and Êzîdxan Asayiş, but also all institutions of the Yazidi community.




“The integration of military forces into Iraq’s security institutions is not a project imposed from outside, but a process that has developed through the will of our people and guarantees the preservation of our achievements and lasting security for our community. Those who seek to portray this as a threat are themselves the ones attempting to profit from our community’s suffering and leave Shengal defenseless once again,” the statement said.

content:

During the years when waves of darkness swept across the world and brutal gangs sought to destroy humanity, Kobanê became the place where the star of freedom rose once again. In its streets, coloured with the blood of heroes, the will of free women demonstrated that no force of darkness could stand against the aspiration for a free life. What made the resistance of Kobanê an unprecedented epic was the unity and national consciousness of our people.

title: MSD: World Kobanê Day carries renewed significance amid deep transformations across Syria
content:
The Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) released a statement marking World Kobanê Day.




Titled “From Resistance to Political Presence,” the statement reads as follows:




“On November 1, the Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) marks World Kobanê Day, reflecting on its profound historical, humanitarian, and political significance. Today, Kobanê and its people play a pivotal role in shaping Syria’s future. In 2014, the resistance of Kobanê transcended geographic borders. It became a global symbol of human resolve against terrorism and a testament to the defense of freedom, dignity, and diversity.




When Kobanê faced ISIS’s brutal offensive, its people made immense sacrifices to protect their city, identity, and right to live. Their resistance marked a critical turning point in the global fight against terrorism. It sparked widespread international solidarity that went beyond supporting a besieged city. Ultimately, Kobanê represented a global stand against violent extremism and a victory for human dignity, freedom, and self-preservation.




The battle of Kobanê proved that the will of the people and their right to self-defense are a vital shield against projects of exclusion and annihilation. title: The Kurdistan Region’s experience of government – III
content:
In the previous part of our series, we examined the common causes of government formation crises that have recurred in the Kurdistan Region over the past three decades, as well as the election process of 20 October 2024. This part examines the demands put forward by the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) in negotiations, the institutional vacuum created by the failure to form a government and the price the people are paying for it.




The KDP's demands




Iraqi media reported that the negotiating delegations of the two parties reached an agreement on 4 February 2025 on a draft joint government programme comprising nine sections and 15 articles. The programme covered parliament, finance, foreign relations, relations between Erbil (Hewlêr) and Baghdad, the peshmerga, energy and the judiciary. However, negotiations over the distribution of government positions lagged behind agreement on the programme.




The KDP's offer expanded over time. In April 2025, the PUK was offered only the ministries of Peshmerga Affairs and Finance. On 6 November 2025, however, the KDP announced that it had offered the PUK the parliamentary speakership, the vice-presidency of the Kurdistan Region, the deputy premiership, eight or nine ministries and "influential positions" within the security institutions.

title: Kurdish doctoral student imprisoned in Iran
content:
Matin Faramarzpour, a Kurdish cultural activist and doctoral student in philosophy at the University of Tabriz, has been sent to Mahabad Prison to serve a six-month sentence for “propaganda against the state”.




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that Faramarzpour, who is from Mahabad, was arrested on 28 October after appearing in response to a summons at the Enforcement of Judgements Office of the city’s Public and Revolutionary Prosecutor’s Office, and transferred to prison.




On 8 July, security forces violently arrested Faramarzpour in Mahabad’s Sheikh Shaltout Park, and he was provisionally released on bail several weeks later.




Branch One of the Islamic Revolutionary Court of Mahabad subsequently sentenced him to six months in prison on charges of “propaganda against the state.”

title: Sancar: Abdullah Öcalan has moved to the new facility built on Imrali
content:
Mithat Sancar, a member of the Imrali Delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), made remarks on current developments during an interview with Medya Haber TV.




Stating that the Peace and Democratic Society Process had experienced a slowdown over the past two months, Sancar said that following the steps taken by the Kurdish Movement, the delegation needed to visit Imrali. He explained that the committee tasked with working with Abdullah Öcalan was the Peace and Politicisation Committee, emphasising that Öcalan's coordination was essential for the process to advance.




Saying that the process could not move forward through one-sided expectations and demands, Sancar stressed that the state needed to abandon its rigid stance in order to overcome the main obstacles.




“The move that will resolve the main deadlock will come from Mr Öcalan. I do not believe there is an issue that cannot be overcome, but for it to be resolved, the state must move away from its persistent and rigid approach,” he said.




Stating that Öcalan's aim was to unite the Kurds as a political subject, Sancar added: “Mr Öcalan has moved to the new facility built on Imrali. His agreement to move there should lead to an acceleration of the process.”

title: Turkish soldiers torture three women from Rojava at the border
content:
Turkish soldiers reportedly detained and assaulted three women at the border between Rojava and Northern Kurdistan, confiscating their money and personal belongings. According to the ANHA news agency, the incident occurred near the village of Qereman in Dirbêsiyê as the women attempted to cross the border from Rojava into Northern Kurdistan.




According to ANHA, the three women were stopped and tortured by Turkish border guards. No information is currently available about their whereabouts or state of health. No further details about the incident have been released so far.




Reports of mistreatment, violent pushbacks, and assaults by Turkish border forces continue to emerge along the Turkish-Syrian border. Human rights organizations have documented cases for years in which people attempting to cross the border have been beaten, shot at, or robbed of their personal belongings. Those particularly affected are people trying to cross the border due to war, persecution, or economic hardship.

title: ‘The National Security Council decision must be overcome and Mr. Öcalan’s status clarified’
content:
The peace process in Turkey, launched following the Call for Peace and a Democratic Society announced publicly by Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February 2025, approaches its second year.  As part of the process, the Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration was adopted by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey on 10 August 2026, with 467 votes in favour. The bill stipulates that certain provisions could be implemented only after assessments by security institutions and confirmation of those assessments through a decision by the National Security Council (MGK).




The Turkish government’s failure to take concrete steps toward legal and political reforms as part of the peace and democratic society process is fueling growing debate and concern about the future of the process. Despite the steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement since the beginning of the process, the state’s failure to fulfill its responsibilities remains one of the obstacles to building mutual trust and advancing a democratic solution.




DEM Party MP Sabahat Erdoğan Sarıtaş spoke to ANF about the current stage of the peace and democratic society process, the government’s responsibilities, and the steps that need to be taken.

title: DEM Party in Mardin calls for fairer budget allocation
content:
The DEM Party has presented its demands for the ongoing budget deliberations in the Turkish parliament in Mardin. During a press briefing in the Artuklu district on Saturday, party representatives criticized the unequal distribution of public funds, growing poverty, and the economic consequences of decades of war policies. The event was held as part of the nationwide “Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice” campaign. Alongside party members, representatives of civil society organizations and other interested individuals attended the meeting.




Mehmet Ali Amak, co-mayor of Artuklu, drew attention to the financial difficulties facing municipalities. He emphasized that many of the city’s problems could only be resolved by providing local administrations with greater financial resources. “We have been in office for more than two years. Our financial situation prevents us from implementing everything we had planned,” Amak explained.




Military spending instead of investment




Nihat Gökalp, co-chair of the DEM Party’s provincial organization in Mardin, linked the budget campaign to the decades-long conflict over the Kurdish question. title: Saturday Mothers commemorate the seven people killed in Mardin in 1995
content:
At their 1,127th vigil in Galatasaray Square in Istanbul, the Saturday Mothers commemorated seven people who disappeared and were murdered in October 1995 after being detained by Turkish soldiers and village guards in the Dargeçit district of Mardin. Three of the victims were minors. Although their remains were discovered in wells years later, the crime has gone unpunished.




The vigil focused on the cases of Davut Altunkaynak (12), Seyhan Doğan (13), Nedim Akyön (16), Mehmet Emin Aslan (19), Abdurrahman Olcay (20), Abdurrahman Coşkun (21), and Süleyman Seyhan (57). The joint statement was read by Gamze Elvan, the sister of Berkin Elvan, who was fatally injured by a police tear gas canister during the Gezi protests in 2013.




Abducted, murdered, and buried in wells




Following the arrests, the families made repeated but unsuccessful attempts to obtain information about the whereabouts of their relatives. At the time, the authorities claimed that those detained had been released after questioning and had subsequently “gone to the mountains.” An initial criminal complaint produced no results. It was not until the families and the Human Rights Association (İHD) submitted a renewed petition on May 29, 2009, that the public prosecutor’s office reopened the investigation.

title: Hundreds demonstrate in Zurich, call for the achievements of the Rojava Revolution to be protected
content:
Around 1,000 people demonstrated in Zurich on Friday evening in defense of the achievements of the Rojava Revolution. Marking World Kobanê Day, they marched through District 4 in response to a call by a regional coalition. Through speeches, a message of solidarity from the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), and a large-scale banner action, participants commemorated the resistance of Kobanê and drew attention to the current challenges facing the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria.




In a communiqué, the Rojava Committee Zurich, which is part of the coalition, described the demonstration as an expression of militant international solidarity. The Committee stated that the resistance of Kobanê, twelve years after the battle against the terrorist organization Islamic State (ISIS), remains as significant as ever. “Especially in times like these, when the profit-driven logic behind the wars waged by those in power is once again being displayed so openly and brutally, the victory in Kobanê remains a symbol of hope and living proof that we can rely only on our own strength,” the committee declared.

title: ‘Labor struggle against capitalism and exploitation’ discussed at women’s conference in Ankara
content:
The second session of the “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, held at the Chamber of Civil Engineers (İMO) of the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB) in Ankara featured discussions under the theme “Labor struggle against capitalism and exploitation.”




The conference is organized at the initiative of 80 women, including journalists, writers, academics, politicians, and activists.




Ayfer Koçak, Co-Chair of the Confederation of Public Employees’ Trade Unions (KESK), said, “If we are to organize against exploitation, we must create a society in which workers can receive what they are entitled to, a society we call a ‘democratic society.’”




Sabahat Tuncel, an activist with the Free Women’s Movement (Tevgera Jinên Azad – TJA), stated that exploitation could not be eliminated without abolishing the capitalist system. “Because this system itself generates inequality and labor exploitation. Consequently, it exploits women’s labor even further. What we really need to focus on is how to eliminate this system.”




Tuncel continued: “As Marx said, ‘Workers are free only insofar as they can sell their labor,’ but even those conditions have now changed. Workers can no longer even sell their labor freely. title: Tahincioğlu: Pressure and access bans on the press are a wake-up call
content:
Pressure on the opposition press has increased under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government, particularly over the past two years. The government has begun using various methods of repression against media outlets it considers critical of its policies.




Access to the website and social media accounts of T24, one of Turkey's most widely read news websites, has been blocked. A trustee was appointed to HALK TV, while the websites and social media accounts of Kurdish media outlets such as Mezopotamya Agency, Jinnews and Yeni Yaşam have frequently faced access restrictions.




Data released by the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) for September 2026 showed that access to 3,492 pieces of online and digital media content had been blocked. During the same period, access restrictions were imposed on 15 news websites, while four websites were shut down.




Journalist Gökçer Tahincioğlu, a representative of T24, assessed the reasons behind the pressure on the press and its impact on journalism.




‘A government that has largely lost its narrative’




Tahincioğlu said that the government had largely lost its political narrative and stressed that the pressure on the press could not be attributed to a single cause. title: Women’s conference in Ankara: There can be no peace without justice
content:
The “Women Discuss the Future Side by Side” conference, organized at the initiative of 80 women, including journalists, writers, academics, politicians, and activists, began in Ankara on. Saturday.




Following the opening speech, the conference continued with musical performances by İlkay Akkaya, Feryal Öney, Nurcan Değirmenci, and Selda Öztürk. More than 500 women from different cities are attending the conference.




Hikmet Kılınç, the mother of İpek Er, who died after being sexually assaulted and driven to suicide by Turkish specialist sergeant Musa Orhan in Siirt, is also among the participants. Showing her daughter’s belongings, photographs, and locks of hair, Hikmet Kılınç said, “I want justice for my daughter.”




The conference, consisting of three sessions, started with its first session, titled “Freedoms, democracy, justice, and equal citizenship.” Speakers at the opening session included politicians Gültan Kışanak and Zeynep Altıok Akatlı, Feride Eralp of the ‘I Need Peace Women’s Initiative’, writer Hidayet Şefkatli Tuksal, and political scientist Füsun Üstel.

title: The Kurdistan Region’s experience of government – II
content:
The expected outcome did not materialise following the elections of 20 October 2024. The two dominant political forces, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), continue to insist on their respective demands. In this part of our series, we examine the government formation crises that have become all too familiar to the people of Southern Kurdistan (Başûr), their causes and the price paid for them.




Deadlocks from the first cabinet to the latest




Each crisis began with a different development, but all reached a deadlock over the same three issues: who would control the region's revenues, who would command the armed forces and intelligence services, and whether the two major parties would be represented equally or according to their parliamentary seats. In 1994, these disputes escalated into war; in 2015, they led to the closure of parliament; and after 2024, they resulted in a prolonged political deadlock.




First cabinet: 

The government was formed on 4 July 1992, 46 days after the elections of 19 May 1992. During this period, efforts were made to overcome allegations of electoral fraud and disagreements over equal representation, with 50 seats for each party.

author: Unknown
title: Iranian regime sentences Kurdish academic to nine years in prison
content:
The Iranian regime’s policies of repression and intimidation targeting the Kurdish population in Rojhilatê Kurdistan continue. Nebî Ûmêd, a university lecturer from the city of Malekshahi (Malekşahî), has been sentenced to nine years in prison for supporting protests held previously.




According to Kolber News, Branch One of the Ilam Province Court of Appeal charged Nebî Ûmêd with “acting against national security, organising gatherings and plotting against national security, and engaging in propaganda against the regime”. The court ruled that five years of his nine-year prison sentence must be served.




The violations of Nebî Ûmêd’s rights have not been limited to his prison sentence. He has been dismissed from his position at Payam Noor University, banned from leaving the country, had his passport confiscated and been prohibited from entering his hometown of Malekşahî.




Nebî Ûmêd is still living in Ilam and has not been allowed to return to his hometown.

title: Prof. Birdal: A system reliant on constant inflows was bound to collapse
content:
The repercussions of the investment fund fraud scandal, which also involves politicians from the Justice and Development Party (AKP), continue, while losses suffered by people seeking to invest their savings and fluctuations in the markets remain subjects of debate.




Professor Murat Birdal, an academic in the Department of Economics at Istanbul University, spoke to ANF about the causes of the fund crisis and its economic consequences.




‘The collapse in gold prices increased interest in funds’




Murat Birdal said that the fund crisis was linked to high inflation in Turkey, explaining that people had turned to investment funds to protect and increase the value of their savings. Birdal noted that savers had sought alternative investment instruments in response to high inflation and described how the situation developed.




Birdal said: "The main issue here is that people were trying to find ways to protect their savings against high inflation. Initially, deposit interest rates were very high, and people directed their money into bank deposits. As interest rates began to fall, people turned to instruments outside the Turkish lira, such as gold. However, when gold prices plummeted, interest in investment funds increased significantly.




Some of these funds are money market funds. They invest in relatively safer instruments such as Treasury bonds, corporate debt securities

author: Unknown
title: Kamuran Reşîd: The greatest injustices occur in prisons
content:
Despite the steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the Turkish government has yet to take any serious action. Human rights violations, unlawful practices and arbitrary measures in prisons continue to increase. Prisoners are being prevented from securing their release by Administrative and Observation Boards, which justify their decisions by citing "forced expressions of remorse" and claims that prisoners are "not ready to reintegrate into society". Political prisoners who have very little time remaining before their scheduled release are prevented from leaving prison through disciplinary penalties or other justifications and continue to be held behind bars.




Kamuran Reşîd, a member of the Rojava Prisoners Committee, spoke to ANF about the situation in prisons. Reşîd began by recalling that Abdullah Öcalan initiated the Peace and Democratic Society Process on 27 February 2025 and said: "The Call for Peace and a Democratic Society presents us with a new way of life, intellectually grounded in Abdullah Öcalan's ideas. Like a light, it opens the door to a new life. His call exposes the problems created by the existing global system and the deadlocks it has produced. Through this call, Abdullah Öcalan intervened in the current process of deadlock, crisis and collapse. He recognised that the existing system was no longer ca

author: Unknown
title: Bilmez: The right to hope is a legal right, not a privilege
content:
The political authorities' delay in taking the necessary steps regarding the Peace and Democratic Society Process has become a subject of debate. Since the process began, Kurdish political representatives and the Kurdish movement have emphasised that clarifying the status of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan and implementing the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) ruling on the right to hope are indispensable conditions for negotiations. However, tensions have arisen following indications that those sentenced before 2005 would not benefit from the Framework Law, as well as statements by Presidential Chief Adviser Mehmet Uçum that Öcalan's status as a convicted prisoner would not change and that the enforcement of his sentence would not be suspended. Ibrahim Bilmez, one of Abdullah Öcalan's lawyers, who submitted another application to the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers last week regarding the right to hope, spoke to ANF. Bilmez emphasised that the right to hope is not a privilege but a legal right that Turkey is obliged to uphold.




‘The right to hope cannot be tied to the process’




Lawyers from Asrın Law Office also responded to statements by government representatives concerning the status of Kurdish People's Leader Abdullah Öcalan, the chief negotiator in the Peace and Democratic Society Process, and the conditions necessary for him to work freely.

author: Unknown
title: KNK Rojava: Kurds have the duty to protect Kobanê’s achievements
content:
The Rojava Representation of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK) issued a statement to mark 1 November, World Kobanê Day.




The statement said: "On the occasion of November 1, World Kobanê Day, we, as the Rojava Representation of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK), extend our heartfelt congratulations to the resistance fighters of Kobanê, the families of the martyrs, the YPG/YPJ fighters, and all the people of Kobanê and Rojava. The liberation of Kobanê was not merely a military victory; it was a historic, political and academic event that created a turning point in the history of the Middle East and the struggle for humanity.




Kobanê demonstrated the defeat of the nation-state paradigm and the victory of the Democratic Nation paradigm. In Kobanê, the myth surrounding the terrorist organisation ISIS, which was supported by regional and international powers, was shattered under the leadership of women. Kobanê showed that the organised will of a people is stronger than all modern weapons and large armies. Kobanê demonstrated to the world that Kurds can not only defend themselves, but can also build a democratic alternative for a new Syria and a democratic Middle East."

title: Ambush on Internal Security Forces leaves one dead and two injured
content:
The Internal Security Forces personnel patrolling Syria’s coastal region were targeted by armed individuals.

In a written statement, the General Directorate of Ports and Customs announced that one of its customs patrols had been targeted in an armed ambush.

The statement confirmed that one person was killed, and two others were injured.

title: From France to Kurdistan: How well do we understand society in transition?
content:
France occupies a special place in the political memory of the modern world. The Enlightenment, the Revolution of 1789, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen gave freedom and equality universal significance. Yet proclaiming rights does not necessarily mean that all social groups can exercise them equally. The Republic’s promise of equality has repeatedly been put to the test by colonialism, class divisions, and discrimination against citizens with migrant backgrounds.




Against this backdrop, the words of jurist and statesman Robert Badinter, who lost his father during the Nazi occupation and played a key role in abolishing the death penalty in 1981, take on particular significance: “France is not the country of human rights, but the country where the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was proclaimed.” The gap between the historical legacy of these rights and contemporary social realities continues to demand critical examination.




The new language of the streets




The protests by students at French secondary schools, which began in mid-September and continued throughout October 2026, offer valuable insights into contemporary French society. Teacher shortages, long school days, overcrowded classrooms, poor conditions in school cafeterias, and anxieties about the future are among the students’ concerns. Some protest signs also reveal
